title: Deploy HyperVault with a Private Container Registry | HyperVault Documentation

Deploy HyperVault with a Private Container Registry

HyperVault is licensed under the HyperVault Software License. An active license is required for production deployments.

This procedure deploys HyperVault on Kubernetes clusters using a private container registry for images while installing Helm charts from the public HyperVault Helm repository.

Use this procedure when your environment has internet access to install Helm charts from helm.min.io but you need to pull container images from a private container registry instead of the public quay.io registry.

This procedure requires installation of Kubernetes operators and associated resources including CustomResourceDefinitions, StatefulSets, and Secrets into new or existing Namespaces. You must perform the operations in this procedure as a user that has broad permissions to create resources within multiple Namespaces.

When to use this procedure

Use this deployment method when:

  • Your Kubernetes cluster has internet access to reach helm.min.io for Helm chart installation.
  • Your organization requires all container images to be pulled from a private container registry instead of public registries, such as for security, compliance, or governance reasons.

Comparison with airgap deployment:

If your Kubernetes cluster is in an airgapped environment with no internet access, use the Deploy HyperVault in an Airgapped Environment procedure instead. That procedure covers copying both Helm charts and container images to private registries for deployment in environments without internet connectivity.

Prerequisites

Before beginning this procedure, ensure you have the following:

  • Kubernetes cluster running an in-support release
  • Helm version 3.17 or later
  • Private container registry accessible from the Kubernetes cluster
  • Network access to copy images from quay.io to the private container registry
  • Skopeo installed for copying container images
  • Valid HyperVault license from SUBNET
  • kubectl configured to access the target Kubernetes cluster
  • Network access to helm.min.io from your deployment environment

Deploy HyperVault using Helm with private container registry

The following procedure copies required container images to a private container registry and deploys HyperVault using Helm charts from the public HyperVault repository.

Copy container images to private registry

Copy mandatory images and any optional images you need from quay.io to your private container registry. Perform these steps from a system that has network access to both quay.io and your private registry.

In each step, replace PRIVATE_REGISTRY with the hostname and path to your private container registry. If you use a different software or method for copying images to your private repository, defer to the documentation or procedure for that tooling.

The following commands use --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 flags to ensure images are copied for Linux AMD64 architecture. If your Kubernetes cluster uses a different architecture (such as ARM64), replace amd64 with the appropriate architecture for your cluster.

If your private registry does not have TLS configured, add the --dest-tls-verify=false flag to each skopeo command. For production environments, configure your registry with proper TLS certificates instead of disabling verification.

  1. Copy the operator image: 

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z

  2. Copy the hypervault image: 

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-08-21T02-50-21Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-08-21T02-50-21Z

  3. Copy the hypervault-sidecar image: 

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-06-30T21-59-04Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-06-30T21-59-04Z

  4. Copy optional images based on the features you plan to use.

    Copy the kes and kes-sidecar images if you plan to use server-side encryption with Key Encryption Service:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/kes:RELEASE.2025-07-15T11-40-19Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/kes:RELEASE.2025-07-15T11-40-19Z

skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/kes-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-07-01T00-09-56Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/kes-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-07-01T00-09-56Z

    Copy the mc image if you plan to automate jobs using the HyperVault Client:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/mc:RELEASE.2025-08-21T03-14-05Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/mc:RELEASE.2025-08-21T03-14-05Z

    Copy the aihub image if you plan to store AI models and datasets:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/aihub:RELEASE.2024-12-13T23-00-47Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/aihub:RELEASE.2024-12-13T23-00-47Z

    Copy the prompt image if you plan to query your objects with generative AI:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/prompt:RELEASE.2025-01-17T21-55-43Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/prompt:RELEASE.2025-01-17T21-55-43Z

    Copy the warp image if you plan to run benchmark tests on your cluster:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/warp:v1.3.0 \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/warp:v1.3.0

  5. Verify that the images are accessible in your private registry.

    You can use skopeo inspect to verify each image was copied successfully:

    skopeo inspect docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z

    If your registry has a REST API endpoint, you can also verify using curl:

    curl -k https://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/v2/_catalog
curl -k https://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/v2/hypervault/operator/tags/list

    Replace https:// with http:// if your registry does not use TLS.

Create image pull secret

If your private container registry requires authentication, create a Kubernetes secret for pulling images.

Create the image pull secret in the hypervault namespace:

kubectl create secret docker-registry private-repo-pull-secret \
  --docker-server=PRIVATE_REGISTRY \
  --docker-username=USERNAME \
  --docker-password=PASSWORD \
  --docker-email=EMAIL \
  -n hypervault

Replace the following values:

  • PRIVATE_REGISTRY: The hostname of your private container registry
  • USERNAME: Username for authenticating to the private container registry
  • PASSWORD: Password for authenticating to the private container registry
  • EMAIL: Email address associated with the container registry account

Add the HyperVault Helm repository

Add the public HyperVault Helm repository to install the HyperVault Helm charts.

helm repo add hypervault https://helm.min.io/
helm repo update

Configure Helm values for private container registry

Create a Helm values file that configures HyperVault to use your private container registry for pulling images.

  1. Retrieve your license file.

    Log in to SUBNET and select the License button in the Deployments view. Save the content of the file in a secure location for use in the next step. You need the decoded JWT token value from the license file (beginning with eyJ...) for installation.

    License Management

    Starting with HyperVault Server RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z, deployments can start without a license in offline mode. All S3 operations are blocked until you install a valid license, but the Admin API and Console remain accessible.

    After deployment starts, you can register with SUBNET and apply your license:

    mc license register ALIAS --license /path/to/hypervault.license

    For license renewal, expiration details, and mode restrictions, see Licenses.

  2. Create a YAML manifest to customize the hypervault/hypervault-operator chart.

    Use your preferred text editor to create a YAML manifest for the chart named hypervault-operator-values.yaml.

    The following YAML example configures the private container registry settings:

    repositories:
  hypervault:
    hostname: PRIVATE_REGISTRY
    pathPrefix: hypervault/
    imagePullSecrets:
    - name: private-repo-pull-secret
  hypervault:
    hostname: PRIVATE_REGISTRY
    pathPrefix: hypervault/
    imagePullSecrets:
    - name: private-repo-pull-secret

    Replace PRIVATE_REGISTRY with the hostname of your private container registry (for example, registry.example.com or registry.example.com:5000).

    The repositories section configures the Helm chart to pull all HyperVault images from your private container registry instead of quay.io. The pathPrefix value specifies the path within your container registry where you copied the images. The imagePullSecrets values specified in each repository configuration are automatically propagated by the operator to all Deployments, StatefulSets, and other resources that use images from that repository.

    Why two repository configurations?

    The configuration includes two repository entries:

    • hypervault: Used for HyperVault-specific images (operator, hypervault, hypervault-sidecar, kes, kes-sidecar, mc, aihub, prompt)
    • hypervault: Used for HyperVault community images (warp)

    This separation allows you to organize images in your private registry using different path structures if needed. In most cases, you can use the same hostname and similar path prefixes for both repositories.

  3. If you need to override specific image versions, add an images section to the hypervault-operator-values.yaml file: 

    images:
  hypervault:
    repository: hypervault
    image: hypervault:RELEASE.2025-08-29T21-27-49Z

    This example overrides the default hypervault image version with a different release. Refer to the HyperVault Operator values reference for all available image customizations and the Operator Environment Variables reference for configuring Operator behavior.

    Do not update values in the object-store-operator configuration map directly, as helm upgrade overwrites them. Instead, always use an custom YAML file such as hypervault-operator-values.yaml to install and upgrade HyperVault.

Install the HyperVault Operator

Install the HyperVault Operator using the customized values file and your SUBNET license.

  1. Install the chart to the hypervault namespace with the customization file and license: 

    helm install hypervault hypervault/hypervault-operator \
  -n hypervault --create-namespace \
  --set license="eyJhbGciOiJFUzM4NCIsInR..." \
  -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

    Replace the license value with your decoded JWT token from SUBNET.

    This installs the hypervault-operator chart from the public HyperVault Helm repository.

    If successful, the command outputs a summary of installed resources.

  2. Validate the installation by running the following command: 

    kubectl get all -n hypervault

    The output should show running pods similar to the following:

    NAME                                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f-hjbp5         1/1     Running   0          4m16s
pod/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85-kmwlv   1/1     Running   0          4m16s

NAME                            TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)    AGE
service/object-store-operator   ClusterIP   10.43.210.230   <none>        4221/TCP   4m16s

NAME                                    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
deployment.apps/adminjob-operator       1/1     1            1           4m16s
deployment.apps/object-store-operator   1/1     1            1           4m16s

NAME                                               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
replicaset.apps/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f         1         1         1       4m16s
replicaset.apps/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85   1         1         1       4m16s

Deploy a HyperVault

After the Operator is running, deploy a HyperVault instance.

  1. Create a YAML manifest to customize the object store chart.

    Use your preferred text editor to create a file named hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml. The following example has a minimal set of fields for deploying an 8x8 object store using HyperVault DirectPV for storage provisioning:

    objectStore:
     name: primary-object-store
     pools:
     - name: pool-0
       servers: 8
       volumesPerServer: 8
       size: 2Ti
     services:
       hypervault:
         serviceType: NodePort
         nodePort: 31000

    Modify the values to reflect your deployment requirements. Remove any default or unmodified values such that the file reflects only your changes.

    Production deployments
    For production deployments, consider enabling PVC protection to prevent accidental data loss. Enable the protection by adding objectStore.pvcProtection: true to your values file.

  2. Install the object store chart: 

    helm install primary-object-store hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -n primary-object-store --create-namespace \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

    This installs the hypervault-objectstore chart from the public HyperVault Helm repository.

    The command deploys a HyperVault with the name and namespace of primary-object-store.

Connect to the deployment

After the object store is deployed, connect to it using either the Console web interface or the HyperVault Client command-line tool.

Configure ingress to route traffic to the -console service in the object store namespace. You can temporarily access the Console using kubectl port-forward:

kubectl port-forward -n primary-object-store svc/primary-object-store-console 9443:9443

You can use the browser interface for managing the object store installation.

  1. Download the mc tool to your local host machine.

    See HyperVault Client Quickstart for installation instructions.

  2. Create a new alias for the HyperVault server.

    The S3 API services are configured via NodePort so you can access them through the IP or hostname of any worker node in the Kubernetes cluster. Use kubectl get nodes -o wide to determine the appropriate IP or hostname to use for access.

    mc --insecure alias set myhypervault https://NODE_IP_OR_HOSTNAME:31000 hypervault hypervault123

    Replace NODE_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with the externally accessible hostname or IP of any worker node in the deployment.

  3. Create a bucket and copy a file to that bucket:

    mc --insecure mb myhypervault/data
mc --insecure cp ~/somefile.txt myhypervault/data

Additional configuration

HyperVault supports the following additional ObjectStore configuration options:

  • To configure HyperVault using environment variables, including secure management of sensitive values with Kubernetes Secrets, see Environment Variable Configuration.
  • To distribute pods across failure domains for improved fault tolerance, see Spread Zone Configuration.
  • For all available Helm chart customization options, see the Object Store Helm Chart reference.

Troubleshooting

Architecture mismatch errors when copying images

If you encounter errors like no image found in image index for architecture when using Skopeo, ensure you are using the --override-os and --override-arch flags with the correct values for your Kubernetes cluster.

The images must match the architecture of your Kubernetes nodes, not the system where you run the skopeo commands. For example, if copying from a Mac to a Linux AMD64 cluster:

skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z

TLS/SSL certificate errors

If you see errors related to certificate verification when copying images, you can use one of the following options depending on your environment:

  1. For development/testing: Add --dest-tls-verify=false to disable TLS verification:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  --dest-tls-verify=false \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z

  2. For production environments: Configure your private registry with valid TLS certificates instead of disabling verification.

Connection refused or EOF errors

If Skopeo cannot connect to your private registry:

  1. Verify the registry is running and accessible:

    curl -k https://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/v2/

    This should return an empty JSON object {} if the registry is accessible.

  2. Check that the hostname and port are correct in your PRIVATE_REGISTRY value.

  3. Verify network connectivity between the system running Skopeo and the private registry.

  4. If using a firewall, ensure the registry port is open.

Images fail to pull in Kubernetes

If images were copied successfully but fail to pull in your Kubernetes cluster:

  1. Verify the image pull secret was created correctly:

    kubectl get secret private-repo-pull-secret -n hypervault

  2. Verify the Helm values file contains the correct registry hostname and image pull secret name.

  3. Check pod events for specific error messages:

    kubectl describe pod POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE

  4. Verify network connectivity from the Kubernetes nodes to the private registry.

CLI Download the mc tool to your local host machine. See AIStor Client Quickstart for installation instructions. Create a new alias for the MinIO AIStor server. The S3 API services are configured via NodePort so you can access them through the IP or hostname of any worker node in the Kubernetes cluster. Use kubectl get nodes -o wide to determine the appropriate IP or hostname to use for access. mc --insecure alias set myaistor https://NODE_IP_OR_HOSTNAME:31000 minio minio123 Replace NODE_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with the externally accessible hostname or IP of any worker node in the deployment. Create a bucket and copy a file to that bucket: mc --insecure mb myaistor/data mc --insecure cp ~/somefile.txt myaistor/data Additional configuration MinIO AIStor supports the following additional ObjectStore configuration options: To configure MinIO AIStor using environment variables, including secure management of sensitive values with Kubernetes Secrets, see Environment Variable Configuration. To distribute pods across failure domains for improved fault tolerance, see Spread Zone Configuration. For all available Helm chart customization options, see the Object Store Helm Chart reference. Troubleshooting Architecture mismatch errors when copying images If you encounter errors like no image found in image index for architecture when using Skopeo, ensure you are using the --override-os and --override-arch flags with the correct values for your Kubernetes cluster. The images must match the architecture of your Kubernetes nodes, not the system where you run the skopeo commands. For example, if copying from a Mac to a Linux AMD64 cluster: skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \ docker://quay.io/minio/aistor/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z \ docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/aistor/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z TLS/SSL certificate errors If you see errors related to certificate verification when copying images, you can use one of the following options depending on your environment: For development/testing: Add --dest-tls-verify=false to disable TLS verification: skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \ --dest-tls-verify=false \ docker://quay.io/minio/aistor/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z \ docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/aistor/operator:RELEASE.2025-08-19T17-53-00Z For production environments: Configure your private registry with valid TLS certificates instead of disabling verification. Connection refused or EOF errors If Skopeo cannot connect to your private registry: Verify the registry is running and accessible: curl -k https://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/v2/ This should return an empty JSON object {} if the registry is accessible. Check that the hostname and port are correct in your PRIVATE_REGISTRY value. Verify network connectivity between the system running Skopeo and the private registry. If using a firewall, ensure the registry port is open. Images fail to pull in Kubernetes If images were copied successfully but fail to pull in your Kubernetes cluster: Verify the image pull secret was created correctly: kubectl get secret private-repo-pull-secret -n aistor Verify the Helm values file contains the correct registry hostname and image pull secret name. Check pod events for specific error messages: kubectl describe pod POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE Verify network connectivity from the Kubernetes nodes to the private registry.

title: Configure Load Balancing | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Configure Load Balancing

HyperVault’s distributed architecture allows any node to handle any request. While clients can connect directly to individual nodes, a load balancer provides a single endpoint that simplifies client configuration and automatically routes traffic to healthy nodes.

Load balancers also centralize SSL/TLS certificate management and can terminate encryption at the network edge, reducing computational overhead on HyperVault nodes.

Prerequisites

Your load balancer configuration must support these HyperVault requirements:

  • Dual-service routing: Configure separate routes for the S3 API (port 9000) and Console UI (port 9001).
  • Streaming uploads: Allow unlimited request body size and disable request buffering to support uploading objects of any size.
  • Streaming downloads: Disable response buffering to support downloading large objects.

Example configurations

These examples show how to implement the prerequisites for common Ingress controllers.

Add these annotations to your Ingress resource:

metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ignore-invalid-headers: "false"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "0"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-request-buffering: "off"

If your HyperVault backend uses HTTPS, also add:

    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS"

For additional NGINX Ingress annotations, see the NGINX Ingress Annotations Reference.

Deprecation warning
Open source Ingress NGINX version has been retired as of March 2026

Add these annotations to your Ingress resource:

metadata:
  annotations:
    haproxy.org/timeout-server: "300s"

HAProxy does not buffer request bodies by default, which supports streaming uploads. Use the backend-config-snippet annotation to add additional HAProxy directives if needed:

    haproxy.org/backend-config-snippet: |
      option http-keep-alive

If your HyperVault backend uses HTTPS, also add:

    haproxy.org/server-ssl: "true"

For additional HAProxy Ingress annotations, see the HAProxy Ingress Controller Documentation.

Configure buffering settings with a Middleware resource:

apiVersion: traefik.io/v1alpha1
kind: Middleware
metadata:
  name: hypervault-buffering
spec:
  buffering:
    maxRequestBodyBytes: 0
    maxResponseBodyBytes: 0

Reference the middleware in your IngressRoute:

apiVersion: traefik.io/v1alpha1
kind: IngressRoute
metadata:
  name: hypervault-s3
spec:
  routes:
    - match: Host(`hypervault.example.com`)
      kind: Rule
      middlewares:
        - name: hypervault-buffering
      services:
        - name: hypervault-hl
          port: 9000

For additional Traefik configuration options, see the Traefik documentation.

Configuration requirements

Configure HyperVault with the appropriate environment variable and DNS settings to ensure proper communication through your load balancer.

Domain-based routing uses separate hostnames for the S3 API and Console UI (recommended for production deployments).

  1. Configure your load balancer or Ingress to route traffic based on hostname:

    • hypervault.example.com → Service port 9000
    • console.hypervault.example.com → Service port 9001

  2. Obtain your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname:

    For Kubernetes deployments using LoadBalancer services:

    kubectl get svc -n primary-object-store

    For Ingress-based deployments, use your Ingress controller’s external endpoint.

  3. Set HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL to your Console UI domain in your HyperVault object store configuration.

    Add the environment variable to your hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file:

    objectStore:
  name: primary-object-store
  env:
    - name: HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL
      value: "https://console.hypervault.example.com"

    Apply the configuration with Helm:

    helm upgrade primary-object-store hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -n primary-object-store \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

Path-based routing uses a single hostname with different paths for the S3 API and Console UI.

  1. Configure your load balancer or Ingress to route traffic based on URL path:

    • / (root path) → Service port 9000 (S3 API)
    • /console → Service port 9001 (Console UI)

  2. Obtain your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname:

    For Kubernetes deployments using LoadBalancer services:

    kubectl get svc -n primary-object-store

    For Ingress-based deployments, use your Ingress controller’s external endpoint.

  3. Set HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL to your Console UI path in your HyperVault object store configuration.

    Add the environment variable to your hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file:

    objectStore:
  name: primary-object-store
  env:
    - name: HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL
      value: "https://hypervault.example.com/console"

    Apply the configuration with Helm:

    helm upgrade primary-object-store hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -n primary-object-store \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

For detailed information about the HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL environment variable and additional console configuration options, see Console Environment Variables.

Verify your configuration

After configuring your load balancer, verify it works correctly using the load balancer’s IP or hostname before updating production DNS.

  1. Test the health endpoint through your load balancer:

    curl https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME/hypervault/health/live

    Expected response: 200 OK with body OK

    Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname.

    For comprehensive health check documentation, see Health Check Probes.

  2. Configure and test the HyperVault Client connection using your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname:

    mc alias set myhypervault https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME ACCESS_KEY SECRET_KEY
mc ping myhypervault
mc ready myhypervault

    Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname, and ACCESS_KEY and SECRET_KEY with appropriate credentials.

  3. Verify Console UI access by opening https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME in your web browser, logging in, and browsing objects.

    Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname.

Update DNS for production

After successfully verifying your load balancer configuration, update your DNS records to point your production endpoints to the load balancer.

Create DNS A or CNAME records pointing to your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname:

  • hypervault.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname (S3 API)
  • console.hypervault.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname (Console UI)

Create a DNS A or CNAME record pointing to your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname:

  • hypervault.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname

Once DNS propagates, clients can access HyperVault through the configured domain names.

title: Enable Network Encryption | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Enable Network Encryption

HyperVault implements Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2+ encryption with support for Server Name Indication (SNI) for selecting relevant TLS certificates in response to client requests.

HyperVault supports two types of certificate management:

  • Automatic TLS certificate provisioning (default)
  • User-provided TLS certificates

When deploying a HyperVault resource, the CRD definition provides a certificates field for controlling certificate generation and behavior. This field is also available in the object store Helm chart.

Automatic certificate management

For Kubernetes clusters with a valid TLS Cluster Signing Certificate, HyperVault by default automatically generates TLS certificates when you deploy or modify an object store using the Kubernetes certificates.k8s.io API. This certificate includes the appropriate DNS Subject Alternate Names (SANs) for the object store Services and Pods.

Kubernetes by default uses the Kubernetes cluster Certificate Authority (CA) to sign and provision certificates. This certificate is typically placed on each Pod at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt such that other applications within the same Kubernetes cluster can create secured connections using Kubernetes DNS.

The Operator also generates its own TLS certificates for secure communication. You can customize this behavior using Operator Environment Variables such as OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED and OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME.

Manual certificate management

The HyperVault CRD definition provides a certificates field for providing user-controlled certificates to the object store.

Create the Secrets as type kubernetes.io/tls in the object store Namespace and specify them when creating the object store resource. The Operator automatically attaches these certificates to the Pods in support of TLS connectivity to hostnames covered by those certificates.

Dynamic certificate updates

The Operator allows dynamic certificate updates without requiring Pod restarts. HyperVault Server RELEASE.2026-02-02T23-40-11Z and later checks the Secrets symlinks to the certificates folder for changes every minute.

When you modify the TLS Secrets referenced by an object store:

  1. The Operator detects the Secret change and triggers a reconciliation.
  2. The Operator signals the HyperVault process to reload its certificates.
  3. HyperVault scans the certificates directory and loads the updated certificates.
  4. Changes take effect without restarting Pods.

If certificate loading fails during a reload, HyperVault continues using the previously loaded certificates and logs the error.

Verify certificate updates

After updating certificates, verify that HyperVault is serving the new certificate:

# Get the service endpoint
SERVICE_HOST=$(kubectl get svc -n NAMESPACE OBJECTSTORE-hl -o jsonpath='{.metadata.name}')

# Check the certificate being served
openssl s_client -connect ${SERVICE_HOST}.NAMESPACE.svc:9000 -servername ${SERVICE_HOST}.NAMESPACE.svc </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject

Replace NAMESPACE with your object store namespace and OBJECTSTORE with your object store name.

The output displays the certificate’s subject and validity dates. Compare these against your expected certificate to confirm the update succeeded.

Supported TLS cipher suites

HyperVault recommends generating ECDSA (for example, NIST P-256 curve) or EdDSA (for example, Curve25519) TLS private keys/certificates due to their lower computation requirements compared to RSA.

HyperVault in FIPS mode supports only the AES-GCM ciphers. FIPS mode excludes CHACHA20_POLY1305 and all CBC cipher suites.

The Operator’s admission webhook has its own certificate. See Operator webhook TLS.

title: Operator webhook TLS | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Operator webhook TLS

The HyperVault Operator runs an internal upgrade webhook server on port 4221. HyperVault pods connect to this webhook during in-pod version updates to download new binaries. This connection requires TLS, and the HyperVault pods must trust the certificate presented by the operator.

How operator autocert works

By default, the operator generates its own TLS certificate using the Kubernetes Certificate Signing Request (CSR) API. The operator creates a CSR with the kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving signer, which the Kubernetes API server signs using the cluster’s kubelet CA.

The resulting certificate is stored in a secret named object-store-operator-tls in the operator namespace.

The operator also loads any secret prefixed with hypervault-ca-tls in its namespace as a trusted CA. This allows the operator to trust certificates issued by external CAs.

When autocert causes trust failures

The kubelet CA that signs the operator’s certificate may not be trusted by the HyperVault pods. This happens when:

  • The HyperVault tenant uses disableAutoCert: true with certificates signed by a different CA
  • The operator certificate renews and gets signed by a CA that the HyperVault pods do not trust
  • The cluster uses a non-standard CSR signer

Symptoms:

  • HyperVault version updates fail with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
  • The operator log shows TLS handshake error from <IP>: remote error: tls: bad certificate
  • The operator log shows Upgrade server Autocert is enabled, starting certificate setup

Using a custom certificate

Disable autocert and provide a certificate signed by the same CA that the HyperVault pods trust.

Supported versions
The OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED and OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME environment variables require Operator chart 5.2.0 or later. Chart 5.2.0 is the version that renamed the chart from hypervault-objectstore-operator to hypervault-operator, so no release of the old chart supports these variables. The global.operator.extraEnv Helm values path is the same in every chart version.

Step 1: Create a certificate

Create a cert-manager Certificate resource in the operator namespace:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: operator-webhook-tls
  namespace: OPERATOR_NAMESPACE
spec:
  secretName: object-store-operator-tls
  issuerRef:
    name: YOUR_ISSUER
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  dnsNames:
    - object-store-operator
    - object-store-operator.OPERATOR_NAMESPACE.svc
    - object-store-operator.OPERATOR_NAMESPACE.svc.cluster.local
  duration: 8760h
  renewBefore: 720h

Replace OPERATOR_NAMESPACE with the namespace where the operator is deployed (for example, objectstore-operator). Replace YOUR_ISSUER with the name of your cert-manager ClusterIssuer or Issuer.

Step 2: Disable autocert

Add the following environment variables to the operator deployment:

env:
  - name: OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED
    value: "on"
  - name: OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME
    value: "object-store-operator-tls"

If using the Helm chart, set these under global.operator.extraEnv in the values file:

global:
  operator:
    extraEnv:
      - name: OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED
        value: "on"
      - name: OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME
        value: "object-store-operator-tls"

Step 3: Restart the operator

The operator pod must restart to pick up the new environment variables and certificate:

kubectl rollout restart deployment object-store-operator -n OPERATOR_NAMESPACE

Step 4: Verify

Check the operator log for confirmation that the custom certificate is loaded:

kubectl logs -n OPERATOR_NAMESPACE deployment/object-store-operator | grep -i "custom certificate\|TLS"

Test the webhook endpoint from a HyperVault pod:

kubectl exec -n TENANT_NAMESPACE POD -c hypervault -- \
    curl -v https://object-store-operator.OPERATOR_NAMESPACE.svc.cluster.local:4221/webhook/v1/update

A successful response returns HTTP 200 with a list of available HyperVault binaries.

Admission webhook configuration

Starting with Operator chart 5.4.0, the admission webhook (used for pod scheduling and spread zone awareness) is configured as an object with additional options. This webhook is separate from the upgrade webhook on port 4221 described above.

operators:
  object-store:
    webhook:
      enabled: true       # set to false to disable the admission webhook
      caBundle: ""         # custom CA bundle (base64 PEM), auto-injected if empty
      replicas: 1          # number of webhook replicas

To disable the admission webhook entirely:

operators:
  object-store:
    webhook:
      enabled: false

operators:
  object-store:
    webhook: true          # set to false to disable
The hypervault-objectstore-operator chart does not include admission webhook configuration.

The global.operator.extraEnv Helm values path is the same in every chart version, including the old hypervault-objectstore-operator chart (4.x-5.1). The TLS environment variables (OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED, OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME) require Operator chart 5.2.0 or later.

For general upgrade procedures, see Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes.

Mount secret refresh

The operator assembles all referenced certificates (from certificates.server, certificates.client, and certificates.trustedCAs in the ObjectStore spec) into a single mount secret named <objectstore-name>-generated in the tenant namespace. This secret is mounted into the HyperVault pods.

If the underlying certificate secrets are updated but the mount secret is not refreshed, the pods continue using outdated certificates.

To force a refresh:

kubectl delete secret OBJECTSTORE_NAME-generated -n TENANT_NAMESPACE

The operator recreates the mount secret from the current certificate secrets and restarts the affected pods.

Related pages

  • Enable Network Encryption for general Kubernetes TLS configuration
  • TLS certificate management with cert-manager for cert-manager setup
  • TLS certificate troubleshooting for diagnosing certificate errors
  • Operator Environment Variables for all operator configuration options

This happens when: The MinIO tenant uses disableAutoCert: true with certificates signed by a different CA The operator certificate renews and gets signed by a CA that the MinIO pods do not trust The cluster uses a non-standard CSR signer Symptoms: MinIO version updates fail with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority The operator log shows TLS handshake error from <IP>: remote error: tls: bad certificate The operator log shows Upgrade server Autocert is enabled, starting certificate setup Using a custom certificate Disable autocert and provide a certificate signed by the same CA that the MinIO pods trust. Supported versions The OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED and OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME environment variables require Operator chart 5.2.0 or later. Chart 5.2.0 is the version that renamed the chart from aistor-objectstore-operator to aistor-operator, so no release of the old chart supports these variables. The global.operator.extraEnv Helm values path is the same in every chart version. Step 1: Create a certificate Create a cert-manager Certificate resource in the operator namespace: apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1 kind: Certificate metadata: name: operator-webhook-tls namespace: OPERATOR_NAMESPACE spec: secretName: object-store-operator-tls issuerRef: name: YOUR_ISSUER kind: ClusterIssuer dnsNames: - object-store-operator - object-store-operator.OPERATOR_NAMESPACE.svc - object-store-operator.OPERATOR_NAMESPACE.svc.cluster.local duration: 8760h renewBefore: 720h Replace OPERATOR_NAMESPACE with the namespace where the operator is deployed (for example, objectstore-operator). Replace YOUR_ISSUER with the name of your cert-manager ClusterIssuer or Issuer. Step 2: Disable autocert Add the following environment variables to the operator deployment: env: - name: OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED value: "on" - name: OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME value: "object-store-operator-tls" If using the Helm chart, set these under global.operator.extraEnv in the values file: global: operator: extraEnv: - name: OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED value: "on" - name: OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME value: "object-store-operator-tls" Step 3: Restart the operator The operator pod must restart to pick up the new environment variables and certificate: kubectl rollout restart deployment object-store-operator -n OPERATOR_NAMESPACE Step 4: Verify Check the operator log for confirmation that the custom certificate is loaded: kubectl logs -n OPERATOR_NAMESPACE deployment/object-store-operator | grep -i "custom certificate\|TLS" Test the webhook endpoint from a MinIO pod: kubectl exec -n TENANT_NAMESPACE POD -c minio -- \ curl -v https://object-store-operator.OPERATOR_NAMESPACE.svc.cluster.local:4221/webhook/v1/update A successful response returns HTTP 200 with a list of available MinIO binaries. Admission webhook configuration Starting with Operator chart 5.4.0, the admission webhook (used for pod scheduling and spread zone awareness) is configured as an object with additional options. This webhook is separate from the upgrade webhook on port 4221 described above. Operator 5.4+ operators: object-store: webhook: enabled: true # set to false to disable the admission webhook caBundle: "" # custom CA bundle (base64 PEM), auto-injected if empty replicas: 1 # number of webhook replicas To disable the admission webhook entirely: operators: object-store: webhook: enabled: false Operator 5.2-5.3 operators: object-store: webhook: true # set to false to disable Old chart (4.x-5.1) The aistor-objectstore-operator chart does not include admission webhook configuration. The global.operator.extraEnv Helm values path is the same in every chart version, including the old aistor-objectstore-operator chart (4.x-5.1). The TLS environment variables (OPERATOR_AUTO_CERT_DISABLED, OPERATOR_CUSTOM_TLS_SECRET_NAME) require Operator chart 5.2.0 or later. For general upgrade procedures, see Upgrade AIStor on Kubernetes. Mount secret refresh The operator assembles all referenced certificates (from certificates.server, certificates.client, and certificates.trustedCAs in the ObjectStore spec) into a single mount secret named <objectstore-name>-generated in the tenant namespace. This secret is mounted into the MinIO pods. If the underlying certificate secrets are updated but the mount secret is not refreshed, the pods continue using outdated certificates. To force a refresh: kubectl delete secret OBJECTSTORE_NAME-generated -n TENANT_NAMESPACE The operator recreates the mount secret from the current certificate secrets and restarts the affected pods. Related pages Enable Network Encryption for general Kubernetes TLS configuration TLS certificate management with cert-manager for cert-manager setup TLS certificate troubleshooting for diagnosing certificate errors Operator Environment Variables for all operator configuration options

title: Enable Server Side Encryption | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Enable Server Side Encryption

Server-Side Encryption (SSE) encrypts objects as HyperVault writes them, protecting your data at rest without requiring clients to encrypt data themselves. SSE also underpins regulatory and compliance requirements around secure locking and erasure of data.

To perform SSE, HyperVault Server connects to a key manager that stores and protects the encryption keys. This page introduces how HyperVault encrypts data, how to choose a key manager, and the encryption types HyperVault supports. When you are ready to enable SSE, follow the procedure for your key manager:

  • Server-Side Encryption with HyperVault KMS — recommended for new deployments.
  • Server-Side Encryption with KES — to connect a supported third-party KMS.

How HyperVault encrypts data

HyperVault uses envelope encryption, a layered approach where keys protect other keys:

  • A master key (also called an external key) is a long-lived key stored in the key manager. HyperVault never holds the plaintext master key on disk — it stays in the key manager.

  • For each object, HyperVault requests a unique data key derived from a master key. It encrypts the object with the data key, then stores only an encrypted copy of the data key in the object metadata. To read the object, HyperVault asks the key manager to decrypt the data key, then decrypts the object.

Because the plaintext master keys exist only inside the key manager, controlling access to the key manager controls access to every object it protects. This property is what makes secure erasure and locking possible.

When you enable SSE, HyperVault also encrypts its own backend — identity and access management (IAM) data, configuration, and other internal state — using the default master key.

After you enable SSE, HyperVault requires access to the key manager and the default master key to decrypt the backend and start. You cannot disable or reset backend encryption once enabled.

For a deeper explanation of the key manager itself, see the HyperVault KMS documentation.

Choose a key manager

HyperVault supports three key managers. Configure exactly one through the server-side encryption settings.

Key manager Use it when Learn more
HyperVault KMS (recommended) You want a dedicated root key manager with native HyperVault integration. This is the default key manager for new deployments. Enable with HyperVault KMS
Key Encryption Service (KES) You must store master keys in a supported third-party KMS, such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Entrust, Fortanix, or Thales. Considered legacy. Enable with KES
Static key You are testing or evaluating SSE. Not for production. HYPERVAULT_KMS_SECRET_KEY

HyperVault KMS provides equivalent functionality to third-party KMS solutions for managing root encryption keys. If you run KES today, you can migrate to HyperVault KMS without re-encrypting your data.

Supported encryption types

HyperVault SSE is feature and API compatible with AWS Server-Side Encryption and supports the following encryption strategies:

HyperVault automatically deploys with SSE-KMS encryption of all objects written to a bucket using a specific external key stored in an external key manager. Clients can override the bucket default by specifying an explicit key as part of the write operation.

For buckets without automatic SSE-KMS encryption, clients can specify a key as part of the write operation instead.

You cannot disable SSE-KMS encryption once enabled. HyperVault encrypts backend data as part of enabling server-side encryption.

SSE-KMS provides more granular and customizable encryption compared to SSE-S3 and SSE-C.

HyperVault supports automatic SSE-S3 encryption of all objects written to a bucket with an external key stored in the external key manager. HyperVault SSE-S3 supports one external key for the entire deployment.

For buckets without automatic SSE-S3 encryption, clients can request SSE encryption as part of the write operation instead.

Clients specify an external key as part of the write operation for an object. HyperVault uses the specified key to perform SSE-S3.

SSE-C does not support bucket-default encryption settings and requires clients to perform all key management operations.

SSE-C requires TLS/HTTPS
SSE-C requires a TLS/HTTPS-enabled deployment. The S3 client transmits the customer-provided encryption key in the HTTP request headers, so the key must never travel over plain HTTP.

SSE-C key rotation

S3 clients can change the client-provided key of an existing object. To rotate the key, the client performs an S3 COPY operation where the copy source and destination are the same object, supplying both the current and new keys in the request headers:

Header Value
X-Amz-Server-Side-Encryption-Customer-Key Base64-encoded new key
X-Amz-Copy-Source-Server-Side-Encryption-Customer-Key Base64-encoded current key

Such a self-COPY request is also known as S3 SSE-C key rotation.

Secure erasure and locking

Because HyperVault needs the encryption key — and therefore the key manager — to decrypt an object, you can securely lock or erase objects by controlling access to the key.

General strategies include, but are not limited to:

  • Seal the key manager so HyperVault can no longer reach any keys. This locks all SSE-KMS and SSE-S3 encrypted objects. The objects remain unreadable as long as the key manager stays sealed.

  • Seal or unmount an encryption key. This locks all SSE-KMS or SSE-S3 encrypted objects protected by that key. The objects remain unreadable as long as the key remains sealed.

  • Delete an encryption key. This renders all SSE-KMS or SSE-S3 encrypted objects protected by the key permanently unreadable. Combining key deletion with data deletion may satisfy regulatory requirements for secure erasure.

    Deleting a key is typically irreversible. Exercise extreme caution before intentionally deleting a master key.

title: Server Side Encryption with HyperVault KMS | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Server Side Encryption with HyperVault KMS

This procedure enables Server-Side Encryption (SSE) on a Kubernetes HyperVault deployment using HyperVault KMS as the key manager. HyperVault KMS is the recommended key manager for new deployments.

For background on how HyperVault encrypts data and the encryption types it supports, see Enable Server-Side Encryption.

Enabling SSE on a HyperVault deployment automatically encrypts the backend data for that deployment using the default encryption key selected during setup.

HyperVault requires access to HyperVault KMS to decrypt the backend and start normally. You can neither disable nor reset encryption of the backend.

Prerequisites

Network encryption (TLS)

HyperVault KMS requires TLS connectivity between client and server to protect cryptographic payloads during transmission.

The HyperVault Operator by default deploys resources with TLS automatically configured. If you manually disabled TLS in the cluster, review the networking tutorial for guidance on re-enabling TLS.

Mutual TLS and network path

HyperVault authenticates to HyperVault KMS with mutual TLS (mTLS), where the client presents its own certificate to the server during the TLS handshake. HyperVault derives that client certificate from the HYPERVAULT_KMS_API_KEY value and presents it on every connection. HyperVault KMS identifies the caller from the public key in the certificate. It does not validate the certificate against a certificate authority (CA), so there is no client CA to configure on the HyperVault KMS side.

The client certificate reaches HyperVault KMS only if nothing along the way terminates TLS. Address HyperVault KMS by its in-cluster Service, which passes the connection through unchanged. If you instead reach HyperVault KMS from outside the cluster or through a proxy, that path must be TCP (Layer 4) passthrough. Do not place HyperVault KMS behind an HTTP or HTTPS (Layer 7) Ingress. A Layer 7 Ingress terminates TLS and opens its own connection to HyperVault KMS, so the client certificate never arrives and requests fail with the following message:

client certificate required: client has not sent any certificate during the TLS handshake
A Layer 7 Ingress can report HyperVault KMS as healthy while every cryptographic call fails. HyperVault KMS accepts requests without a client certificate on four routes: /version, /v1/health/live, /v1/health/ready, and /v1/health/metrics. Health checks and metrics scrapes therefore succeed, while every request to /v1/kms returns the error above.

HyperVault KMS

This procedure assumes you have an existing HyperVault KMS deployment. See the HyperVault KMS documentation for guidance on installation and configuration.

From that tutorial you need the HyperVault KMS server endpoints and three resources. Create the resources in the order listed, because each one depends on the previous:

  1. An enclave dedicated to this object store. An enclave is an isolated namespace within HyperVault KMS that holds its own keys and identities. Create it with the minkms add-enclave command.

  2. An administrator identity scoped to that enclave, created with the minkms add-identity command and its --admin flag. The command prints an API key once and cannot display it again, so record it before continuing. Do not reuse the HyperVault KMS cluster administrator API key. HyperVault logs a warning at startup if the API key it receives has SysAdmin privileges.

  3. A default SSE key inside that enclave, created with the minkms add-key command.

Each value maps onto one of the environment variables you set later in this procedure:

Value from HyperVault KMS Environment variable
HyperVault KMS server endpoints HYPERVAULT_KMS_SERVER
Enclave name HYPERVAULT_KMS_ENCLAVE
API key of the enclave administrator identity HYPERVAULT_KMS_API_KEY
Default SSE key name HYPERVAULT_KMS_SSE_KEY

Procedure

This procedure uses Helm and assumes an existing HyperVault deployment

  1. Retrieve the current Chart values

    Use the helm get values command to retrieve the current Chart values.yaml:

    helm get values OBJECT-STORE-NAME -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE -o yaml > hypervault-object-store-name-values.yaml

    Create a backup of the file with the -bak.yaml suffix for records. If you use Git or a similar version control technology, you can use that system for retrieving the values file instead.

    Review the value of objectStore.configuration.name. This name points to the secret containing the object store configuration file in the namespace and is required in the next step. If you did not override this value, it defaults to myhypervault-env-configuration.

  2. Retrieve the configuration secret.

    Create a local copy of the secret using the kubectl get command:

    kubectl get secret/myhypervault-env-configuration -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE -o yaml > myhypervault-env-configuration.yaml

    Replace the myhypervault-env-configuration with the value of objectStore.configuration.name from your Helm chart.

  3. Retrieve the configuration

    The data.config.env field in the secret contains the base64-encoded configuration. The following command uses the yq and base64 utilites to decode and save the file:

    yq -r '.data."config.env"' myhypervault-env-configuration.yaml | base64 -d > myhypervault-env-configuration

    The file contains any environment variables previously set or configured for the object store.

  4. Add HyperVault KMS settings to the environment file

    Open the myhypervault-env-configuration file in your preferred text editor and add the following lines:

     # HyperVault KMS settings

 # Provide the address of the HyperVault KMS Service in your Kubernetes cluster.
 # Replace KMS-RELEASE-NAME and KMS-NAMESPACE with the Helm release name and namespace of your HyperVault KMS deployment.
 # Any other path must pass TLS through unchanged, or mutual TLS authentication breaks.

 HYPERVAULT_KMS_SERVER="https://KMS-RELEASE-NAME-minkms.KMS-NAMESPACE.svc.cluster.local:7373"

 # Specify the name for the default encryption key
 # This key is used for backend and default bucket encryption.
 # Consider specifying a unique key name to facilitate easy identification among other stored keys.
 #
 # Do not modify the HYPERVAULT_KMS_SSE_KEY value after setup.
 # HyperVault requires this key to start successfully.

 HYPERVAULT_KMS_SSE_KEY="object-store-primary-default-key"

 # Specify the HyperVault KMS enclave to use

 HYPERVAULT_KMS_ENCLAVE="object-store-primary"

 # Specify the HyperVault KMS API key to use for authenticating operations.
 # The API key must have permission to access and perform operations in the HyperVault KMS enclave

 HYPERVAULT_KMS_API_KEY="k1:APIKEYSTRING"

  5. Update the secret YAML

    Re-encode the updated environment file using base64 and replace the data.config.env value.

  6. Re-apply the secret

    Use kubectl apply to apply the secret and update the configuration setting in the Namespace.

  7. Restart HyperVault

    Delete all HyperVault StatefulSets to update the configurations for all Pods simultaneously. Use kubectl delete sts/...

  8. Enable bucket default encryption

    Use the mc CLI tool to connect to the HyperVault deployment. Use the mc encrypt set command to set bucket default encryption.

    For example:

    mc mb object-store-k8s/data
mc encrypt set sse-kms object-store-k8s/data

    To encrypt a bucket with a dedicated key instead of the default key, create the key with mc admin kms key create first:

    mc admin kms key create object-store-k8s data-bucket-encryption-key
mc mb object-store-k8s/data
mc encrypt set sse-kms data-bucket-encryption-key object-store-k8s/data

title: Server Side Encryption with KES | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Server Side Encryption with KES

This page enables Server-Side Encryption (SSE) on a Kubernetes HyperVault deployment using the Key Encryption Service (KES) to connect a supported third-party KMS. For instructions on running KES, see the KES docs.

For background on how HyperVault encrypts data and the encryption types it supports, see Enable Server-Side Encryption.

KES is legacy
KES is the legacy path for integrating a third-party KMS. New deployments should use HyperVault KMS instead. If you already run KES, you can migrate to HyperVault KMS without re-encrypting your data.

Enabling SSE on a HyperVault deployment automatically encrypts the backend data for that deployment using the default encryption key.

HyperVault requires access to KES and the external KMS to decrypt the backend and start normally. The KMS must maintain access to the HYPERVAULT_KMS_KES_KEY_NAME. You cannot disable or reset encryption of the backend.

Prerequisites

  • The HyperVault Kubernetes Operator deployed on your Kubernetes cluster.

  • Object store services and pods accessible from your local host, to support management with the HyperVault Client (mc).

    For internal hosts, use the service DNS name. For external hosts, specify the hostname of the service exposed by Ingress, Load Balancer, or other Kubernetes network control component.

  • An existing KMS installation accessible from your cluster.

    For deployments on the same cluster as your object store, you can use Kubernetes Service names to connect the object store with the KMS service.

    For external deployments, you must make sure the cluster supports communications between Kubernetes services and pods and the external network. This may require configuring or deploying additional Kubernetes network components or enabling access to the public internet.

Refer to the installation instructions for your supported KMS target to deploy KES and connect it to a KMS solution:

  • AWS Secrets Manager
  • Azure KeyVault
  • Entrust KeyControl
  • Fortanix SDKMS
  • Google Cloud Secret Manager
  • HashiCorp Vault
  • Thales CipherTrust Manager (formerly Gemalto KeySecure)

Procedure

  1. Generate a new encryption key.

    If needed, unseal the backing vault instance before you create a new key. See the documentation for your KMS solution.

    Run the mc admin kms key create command against the object store:

    # Replace my-new-key with the name of the key you want to use for SSE-KMS
mc admin kms key create k8s encrypted-bucket-key

  2. Enable SSE-KMS for a bucket

    You can use either the console or the HyperVault Client to enable bucket-default SSE-KMS with the generated key:

    1. In the Console UI, create a new bucket. Or, select an existing bucket.

    2. In the left-hand menu, select Encryption, provide the required information, and select Save.

    3. Add a file to the bucket, and confirm the associated encryption metadata.

    Create a new alias for the HyperVault Server. You can then run mc encrypt set to enable SSE-KMS encryption for a bucket:

    mc alias set k8s https://hypervault.hypervault-tenant-1.svc.cluster-domain.example:443 ROOTUSER ROOTPASSWORD

mc mb k8s/encryptedbucket
mc encrypt set SSE-KMS encrypted-bucket-key k8s/encryptedbucket

    For clients external to the Kubernetes cluster, specify the hostname of the service exposed by Ingress, Load Balancer, or similar Kubernetes network control component.

    Write a file to the bucket using mc cp or any S3-compatible SDK with a PutObject function. You can then run mc stat on the file to confirm the associated encryption metadata.

title: Enable FIPS Mode | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Enable FIPS Mode

Enable FIPS 140-3 ready cryptography for HyperVault deployments on Linux.

When enabled, FIPS mode restricts cryptographic operations to algorithms that align with the Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 140-3 program. Organizations subject to U.S. federal government compliance requirements, or those with similar regulatory needs, may require FIPS-aligned cryptography.

HyperVault FIPS mode uses Go’s native cryptographic module, which restricts operations to FIPS 140-3 approved algorithms. HyperVault makes no statements or representations regarding FIPS 140-3 certification status. Evaluate whether this implementation meets your specific compliance requirements.

Overview

HyperVault uses Go 1.24’s native FIPS 140-3 cryptographic module. Enable FIPS mode at runtime with the GODEBUG environment variable. There is no separate binary required.

With FIPS mode enabled, the following apply:

  • TLS connections use only AES-GCM cipher suites (CHACHA20-POLY1305 is excluded).
  • Object encryption (DARE) uses only AES-256-GCM.
  • SSH/SFTP connections exclude weak key exchange algorithms and non-compliant ciphers.
  • JWT operations use FIPS-validated SHA3 implementations.

Enable FIPS mode

FIPS mode requires setting the GODEBUG environment variable in the HyperVault environment file on all nodes in the deployment.

  1. Open the environment file

    Edit /etc/default/hypervault on each node:

    sudo vi /etc/default/hypervault

  2. Add the GODEBUG variable

    Add the following line to enable FIPS mode:

    GODEBUG="fips140=on"

    The environment file should look similar to:

    # HyperVault Server environment file

HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="/mnt/data-{1...4}"
HYPERVAULT_OPTS="--console-address :9001"
HYPERVAULT_ROOT_USER=admin
HYPERVAULT_ROOT_PASSWORD=hypervaultsecretkey

# Enable FIPS 140-3 mode
GODEBUG="fips140=on"

  3. Apply the change to all nodes

    Copy the updated environment file to all nodes in the deployment. The contents must be identical across all nodes.

    Use a utility like shasum to verify the files match:

    shasum /etc/default/hypervault

  4. Restart HyperVault

    Restart the HyperVault service on all nodes:

    sudo systemctl restart hypervault

    Or use the mc CLI to restart all nodes simultaneously:

    mc admin service restart ALIAS

Verify FIPS mode

Connect to the deployment and check the server information:

mc admin info ALIAS

The output indicates FIPS mode status in the server details.

You can also check the service logs for FIPS indicators:

journalctl -u hypervault | grep -i fips

FIPS mode cipher restrictions

The following tables summarize which cryptographic algorithms are available in FIPS mode versus standard mode.

TLS cipher suites

Cipher Suite Standard Mode FIPS Mode
TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 (TLS 1.3) ✓ ✓
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (TLS 1.3) ✓ ✓
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 (TLS 1.3) ✓ ✗
TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 ✓ ✓
TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 ✓ ✓
TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 ✓ ✓
TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 ✓ ✓
TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305 ✓ ✗
TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305 ✓ ✗

Object encryption (DARE)

Algorithm Standard Mode FIPS Mode
AES-256-GCM ✓ ✓
CHACHA20-POLY1305 ✓ ✗

Public key algorithms

Algorithm Standard Mode FIPS Mode
RSA (2048-4096 bit) ✓ ✓
ECDSA (P-256, P-384, P-521) ✓ ✓
EdDSA/Ed25519 ✓ ✗

Considerations

Certificate compatibility

Ensure your TLS certificates use FIPS-compatible algorithms. Certificates signed with EdDSA/Ed25519 are not compatible with FIPS mode. Use ECDSA with NIST P-256/P-384/P-521 curves or RSA keys instead.

Client compatibility

Clients connecting to a FIPS-enabled deployment must support the available cipher suites. Modern TLS clients generally support AES-GCM cipher suites, but verify compatibility with older clients if necessary.

Performance

AES-GCM cipher suites benefit from hardware acceleration on most modern CPUs (AES-NI instruction set). Performance impact from enabling FIPS mode is typically minimal on hardware with AES-NI support.

Related resources

  • Enable Network Encryption for TLS configuration
  • Server Side Encryption for encryption at rest

title: Install HyperVault | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Install HyperVault

HyperVault is licensed under the HyperVault Software License. Production clusters require an active license.

Install on Red Hat Enterprise Linux

Deploy HyperVault onto RHEL 10+

Install on Ubuntu Server

Deploy HyperVault onto Ubuntu 24.04.02 LTS+

These guides deploy HyperVault onto Linux infrastructure. Complete one of them first, then enable network encryption and server-side encryption.

Before you deploy, review the HyperVault Release Notes to find the latest stable release and any version-specific considerations. Each release includes a software bill of materials (SBOM) and dependency artifacts for compliance auditing. See Release Artifacts for details.

Linux kernel requirements

HyperVault strongly recommends Linux kernel 6.8 or later for all production clusters. Kernel 6.8 and later improves performance in four ways that matter for high-throughput object storage:

  • Faster network stack for distributed workloads
  • Higher NVMe and direct I/O throughput
  • Online XFS repair
  • Less memory fragmentation and lower scheduling latency

HyperVault evaluates older kernel versions case by case for existing clusters that cannot upgrade yet. Request an architecture review through SUBNET before you deploy on a kernel earlier than 6.8.

Recommended Linux distributions

Distribution Default Kernel Notes
Ubuntu 24.04 LTS 6.8 Recommended for production
RHEL 10 6.12 Recommended for production
Rocky Linux 10 6.12 Recommended for production
AlmaLinux 10 6.12 Recommended for production
Debian 13 (Trixie) 6.12 Recommended when GA available
Oracle Linux 10 6.12 Recommended for production
SUSE Linux 15 SP7 6.4 Check for kernel updates

Production hardware

When you select hardware for HyperVault, consider these factors:

  • How much data you store at launch, and how much you expect to add over the next two years, to size total drive capacity
  • The number of objects, grouped by average object size
  • How long you retain data, in years
  • The number of sites
  • The number of buckets
  • How many drive and node failures you must tolerate

No single formula fits every situation. Weigh these factors against your own needs, then open an architecture review in SUBNET to work through them with HyperVault engineers and field architects.

Hardware consistency

HyperVault, like any distributed system, performs best when every node in a server pool has an identical configuration. Match the hardware (CPU, memory, motherboard, storage adapters) and the software (operating system, kernel settings, system services) across all nodes in a pool.

Performance can become unpredictable when nodes differ.

Checklist

This checklist follows HyperVault’s Recommended Configuration for production clusters. Treat it as a baseline. It does not replace SUBNET Performance Diagnostics, Architecture Reviews, and direct-to-engineering support.

Component Requirement Recommended
Hosts Dedicated bare-metal or virtual hosts 8+ dedicated hosts
Storage Dedicated locally-attached drives for each host 8+ drives per HyperVault Server
Network High speed network infrastructure 100GbE
CPU Server-grade CPUs with support for modern SIMD instructions (AVX-512), such as Intel® Xeon® Scalable or better 16+ CPU/socket or vCPU per host
Memory Available memory to meet or exceed per-server usage by a reasonable buffer 128GB+ of available memory per host

HyperVault can run on less than the recommended hardware, but the cost savings come at the risk of lower reliability, lower performance, or reduced functionality.

Optimizing performance

These three areas have the greatest impact on HyperVault performance, in order of importance. Secure the components in each area before you address other hardware resources, such as compute constraints.

Infrastructure segment Description
Network Infrastructure Insufficient or limited throughput constrains performance
Storage Controller Old firmware, limited throughput, or failing hardware constrains performance and affects reliability
Storage (Drive) Old firmware, or slow/aging/failing hardware constrains performance and affects reliability

Additional recommendations

For other requirements, including for networking and memory, see recommended and system requirements.

For reviewing your existing hardware with tests, see recommended hardware tests.

title: Install HyperVault on Red Hat Enterprise Linux | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Install HyperVault on Red Hat Enterprise Linux

HyperVault is licensed under the HyperVault Software License. An active license is required for production deployments.

This procedure downloads and installs the HyperVault Server onto bare-metal hosts running Red Hat Enterprise Linux

Review the Hardware and System Requirements to ensure your target infrastructure meets our guidance. You can also open a SUBNET issue to request an architecture review or assistance during deployment.

HyperVault strongly recommends using only RHEL releases in the Full Support lifecycle with Long-Term Support (LTS) Kernels in the 6.12 or later release series, such as RHEL 10. See Linux Kernel Requirements for recommended distributions and performance details.

Procedure

Repeat these steps for each node in the deployment.

  1. Download the HyperVault Server RPM package

    HyperVault provides a RPM package for the AMD64 and ARM64 architectures. Download the package that reflects the host system’s architecture:

    curl --progress-bar -L dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-amd64/hypervault.rpm -o hypervault.rpm
sudo dnf install hypervault.rpm

    curl --progress-bar -L dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-arm64/hypervault.rpm -o hypervault.rpm
sudo dnf install hypervault.rpm

    You can validate the installation by running hypervault --version.

    The RPM package creates a new systemd unit file for the HyperVault Server. Run systemctl status hypervault to validate the installation of the systemd file.

  2. Retrieve your license file

    Log into SUBNET and select the License button in the Deployments view.

    Create the /opt/hypervault directory if it does not exist. Download the file to /opt/hypervault/hypervault.license and set the ownership to hypervault-user:

    sudo mkdir /opt/hypervault
sudo touch /opt/hypervault/hypervault.license
sudo chown -R hypervault-user:hypervault-user /opt/hypervault

    Edit the hypervault.license file and replace its contents with the license string from the previous step.

    License Management

    Starting with HyperVault Server RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z, deployments can start without a license in offline mode. All S3 operations are blocked until you install a valid license, but the Admin API and Console remain accessible.

    After deployment starts, you can register with SUBNET and apply your license:

    mc license register ALIAS --license /path/to/hypervault.license

    For license renewal, expiration details, and mode restrictions, see Licenses.

  3. Review the environment file

    The RPM installs an environment file to /etc/default/hypervault automatically. Review the contents of the file and modify as directed based on your preferred topology:

    Free tier license restriction
    HyperVault hypervault.RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z or later adds support for HyperVault Free licenses. Clusters using the HyperVault Free license support only single-node single-drive and single-node multi-drive patterns. 
    # Copy the value of your SUBNET license below

HYPERVAULT_LICENSE="/opt/hypervault/hypervault.license"

# Define the expected topology of the deployment
#
# The following is a multi-node multi-drive "distributed" deployment pattern
# that supports high performance, high availability, and large storage requirements
#
# HyperVault recommends distributed topologies for production workloads.
#
# The command includes the port that each Server listens on
# (default 9000).

HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="http://hypervault-{1...4}.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...4}/hypervault"

    # Copy the value of your SUBNET license below

HYPERVAULT_LICENSE="/opt/hypervault/hypervault.license"

# Define the expected topology of the deployment
#
# The following is a single-node multi-drive deployment pattern
# appropriate for storage workloads where distributed performance and
# high availability are not requirements.
#
# The command includes the port that each Server listens on
# (default 9000).

HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="http://hypervault.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...4}/hypervault"

    # Copy the value of your SUBNET license below

HYPERVAULT_LICENSE="/opt/hypervault/hypervault.license"

# Define the expected topology of the deployment
#
# The following is a single-node single-drive deployment pattern
# appropriate for workloads where distributed performance and
# high availability are not requirements.
#
# Single-Node Single-Drive Startup
HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="/mnt/drive-1/hypervault"

    For distributed deployments, all nodes must have matching /etc/default/hypervault environment files. Use a utility such as shasum -a 256 /etc/default/hypervault on each node to verify an exact match across all nodes.

  4. Ensure HyperVault has ownership of associated folders and drives.

    The hypervault.service file runs as the hypervault-user user and group by default. This user must have read/write/access permissions to all files, folders, and drive paths provided to the server process. The RPM installation creates the user and group by default.

    Use the chown and chmod commands to ensure the hypervault-user user and group have the necessary ownership and access permissions. For example:

    chown -R hypervault-user:hypervault-user /opt/hypervault/

# Change this to reflect the series of volumes specified
# to the HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES environment variable
#
# This assumes you have already mounted the drives at the given path
chown -R hypervault-user:hypervault-user /mnt/drive-{1..4}

    Repeat this step for each node in the deployment.

  5. Enable and start the HyperVault deployment.

    Use systemctl enable hypervault.service and systemctl start hypervault to enable and start the server process, respectively.

    systemctl enable hypervault.service && systemctl start hypervault
    RHEL 8 and older systemd
    On RHEL 8 the installed systemd is version 239, which predates the ProtectProc= directive introduced in systemd 247. If the hypervault.service unit includes ProtectProc=invisible, the service fails to start on these hosts. Remove the ProtectProc=invisible line from the [Service] section of the unit, then run systemctl daemon-reload before starting the service.

    You can track the status of the startup using journalctl -u hypervault on each node.

    On successful startup, each hypervault process emits output to the log resembling the following:

    HyperVault Enterprise HyperVault Server
Copyright: 2015-2024 HyperVault, Inc.
Version: RELEASE.YYYY-MM-DDTHH-SS-mmZ (go1.22.4 linux/amd64)

API: https://hypervault-1.example.net:9000 https://203.0.113.10:9000 https://127.0.0.1:9000
    RootUser: hypervaultadmin
    RootPass: hypervaultadmin

WebUI: https://hypervault-1.example.net:9001 https://203.0.113.10:9001 https://127.0.0.1:9001
    RootUser: hypervaultadmin
    RootPass: hypervaultadmin

CLI: https://docs.min.io/hypervault/reference/cli/#quickstart
    $ mc alias set 'myhypervault' 'https://hypervault-1.example.net:9000' 'hypervaultadmin' 'hypervaultadmin'

Docs: https://docs.min.io/hypervault/
Status:         4 Online, 0 Offline.
    The HyperVault hypervault service does not automatically start on host reboot. You must use systemctl enable hypervault.service to start the process as part of the host boot.

  6. Install the HyperVault Client (mc) 

    wget https://dl.min.io/hypervault/mc/release/linux-amd64/mc -O mc
chmod +x ./mc
mv ./mc /usr/local/bin/

mc --version

    wget https://dl.min.io/hypervault/mc/release/linux-arm64/mc -O mc
chmod +x ./mc
mv ./mc /usr/local/bin

mc --version

  7. Connect to the Deployment

    You can connect to the deployment using the built-in Console UI or the HyperVault Client (mc).

    Open your browser to the hostname and port of any node in the deployment. The WebUI output from the previous step indicates which hostnames and ports the hypervault process listens on.

    Log in using the default hypervaultadmin:hypervaultadmin username and password.

    1. Create a new alias for the HyperVault server:

      mc alias set myhypervault http://hypervault.example.net:9000 hypervaultadmin hypervaultadmin

      Replace the URL with the hostname of any node in the deployment or a load balancer, reverse proxy, or similar network control plane component managing connections to the deployment.
