title: Install HyperVault on Ubuntu Server | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Install HyperVault on Ubuntu Server

HyperVault is licensed under the HyperVault Software License. An active license is required for production deployments.

This procedure downloads and installs the HyperVault Server onto bare-metal hosts running Ubuntu Server Linux.

Review the Hardware and System Requirements to ensure your target infrastructure meets our guidance. You can also open a SUBNET issue to request an architecture review or assistance during deployment.

HyperVault strongly recommends using only Long-Term Support (LTS) Ubuntu releases in the LTS standard security maintenance lifecycle with a Linux Kernel version 6.8 or later, such as Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. See Linux Kernel Requirements for recommended distributions and performance details.

Procedure

Repeat these steps for each node in the deployment.

  1. Download the HyperVault Server .deb package

    HyperVault provides a .deb package for the AMD64 and ARM64 architectures. Download the package that reflects the host system’s architecture:

    curl --progress-bar -L dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-amd64/hypervault.deb -o hypervault.deb
sudo dpkg -i hypervault.deb

    curl --progress-bar -L dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-arm64/hypervault.deb -o hypervault.deb
sudo dpkg -i hypervault.deb

    You can validate the installation by running hypervault --version.

    The DEB package creates a new systemd unit file for the HyperVault Server. Run systemctl status hypervault to validate the installation of the systemd file.

  2. Retrieve your license file

    Log into SUBNET and select the License button in the Deployments view.

    Create the /opt/hypervault directory if it does not exist. Download the file to /opt/hypervault/hypervault.license and set the ownership to hypervault-user:

    sudo mkdir /opt/hypervault
sudo touch /opt/hypervault/hypervault.license
sudo chown -R hypervault-user:hypervault-user /opt/hypervault

    Edit the hypervault.license file and replace its contents with the license string from the previous step.

    License Management

    Starting with HyperVault Server RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z, deployments can start without a license in offline mode. All S3 operations are blocked until you install a valid license, but the Admin API and Console remain accessible.

    After deployment starts, you can register with SUBNET and apply your license:

    mc license register ALIAS --license /path/to/hypervault.license

    For license renewal, expiration details, and mode restrictions, see Licenses.

  3. Review the environment file

    The RPM installs an environment file to /etc/default/hypervault automatically. Review the contents of the file and modify as directed based on your preferred topology.

    Free tier license restriction
    HyperVault hypervault.RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z or later adds support for HyperVault Free licenses. Clusters using the HyperVault Free license support only single-node single-drive and single-node multi-drive patterns. 
    # Copy the value of your SUBNET license below

HYPERVAULT_LICENSE="/opt/hypervault/hypervault.license"

# Define the expected topology of the deployment
#
# The following is a multi-node multi-drive "distributed" deployment pattern
# that supports high performance, high availability, and large storage requirements
#
# HyperVault recommends distributed topologies for production workloads.
#
# The command includes the port that each Server listens on
# (default 9000).

HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="http://hypervault-{1...4}.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...4}/hypervault"

    # Copy the value of your SUBNET license below

HYPERVAULT_LICENSE="/opt/hypervault/hypervault.license"

# Define the expected topology of the deployment
#
# The following is a single-node multi-drive deployment pattern
# appropriate for storage workloads where distributed performance and
# high availability are not requirements.
#
# The command includes the port that each Server listens on
# (default 9000).

HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="http://hypervault.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...4}/hypervault"

    # Copy the value of your SUBNET license below

HYPERVAULT_LICENSE="/opt/hypervault/hypervault.license"

# Define the expected topology of the deployment
#
# The following is a single-node single-drive deployment pattern
# appropriate for workloads where distributed performance and
# high availability are not requirements.
#
# Single-Node Single-Drive Startup
HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="/mnt/drive-1/hypervault"

    For distributed deployments, all nodes must have matching /etc/default/hypervault environment files. Use a utility such as shasum -a 256 /etc/default/hypervault on each node to verify an exact match across all nodes.

  4. Ensure HyperVault has ownership of associated folders and drives.

    The hypervault.service file runs as the hypervault-user user and group by default. This user must have read/write/access permissions to all files, folders, and drive paths provided to the server process. The RPM installation creates the user and group by default.

    Use the chown and chmod commands to ensure the hypervault-user user and group have the necessary ownership and access permissions. For example:

    chown -R hypervault-user:hypervault-user /opt/hypervault/

# Change this to reflect the series of volumes specified
# to the HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES environment variable
#
# This assumes you have already mounted the drives at the given path
chown -R hypervault-user:hypervault-user /mnt/drive-{1..4}

    Repeat this step for each node in the deployment.

  5. Enable and start the HyperVault deployment.

    Use systemctl enable hypervault.service and systemctl start hypervault to enable and start the server process respectively.

    You can track the status of the startup using journalctl -u hypervault on each node.

    On successful startup, each hypervault process emits output to the log resembling the following:

    HyperVault Enterprise HyperVault Server
Copyright: 2015-2024 HyperVault, Inc.
Version: RELEASE.YYYY-MM-DDTHH-SS-mmZ (go1.22.4 linux/amd64)

API: https://hypervault-1.example.net:9000 https://203.0.113.10:9000 https://127.0.0.1:9000
    RootUser: hypervaultadmin
    RootPass: hypervaultadmin

WebUI: https://hypervault-1.example.net:9001 https://203.0.113.10:9001 https://127.0.0.1:9001
    RootUser: hypervaultadmin
    RootPass: hypervaultadmin

CLI: https://docs.min.io/hypervault/reference/cli/#quickstart
    $ mc alias set 'myhypervault' 'https://hypervault-1.example.net:9000' 'hypervaultadmin' 'hypervaultadmin'

Docs: https://docs.min.io/hypervault/
Status:         4 Online, 0 Offline.
    The HyperVault hypervault service does not automatically start on host reboot. You must use systemctl enable hypervault.service to start the process as part of the host boot.

  6. Install the HyperVault Client (mc) 

    wget https://dl.min.io/hypervault/mc/release/linux-amd64/mc -O mc
chmod +x ./mc
mv ./mc /usr/local/bin/

mc --version

    wget https://dl.min.io/hypervault/mc/release/linux-arm64/mc -O mc
chmod +x ./mc
mv ./mc /usr/local/bin

mc --version

  7. Connect to the Deployment

    You can connect to the deployment using the built-in Console UI or the HyperVault Client (mc).

    Open your browser to the hostname and port of any node in the deployment. The WebUI output from the previous step indicates which hostnames and ports the hypervault process listens on.

    Log in using the default hypervaultadmin:hypervaultadmin username and password.

    1. Create a new alias for the HyperVault server:

      mc alias set myhypervault http://hypervault.example.net:9000 hypervaultadmin hypervaultadmin

      Replace the URL with the hostname of any node in the deployment or a load balancer, reverse proxy, or similar network control plane component managing connections to the deployment.

    2. Create a bucket and copy a file to that bucket:

      mc mb myhypervault/data
mc cp ~/somefile.txt myhypervault/data

title: Configure Load Balancing | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Configure Load Balancing

HyperVault’s distributed architecture allows any node to handle any request. While clients can connect directly to individual nodes, a load balancer provides a single endpoint that simplifies client configuration and automatically routes traffic to healthy nodes.

Load balancers also centralize SSL/TLS certificate management and can terminate encryption at the network edge, reducing computational overhead on HyperVault nodes.

Prerequisites

Your load balancer configuration must support these HyperVault requirements:

  • Dual-service routing: Configure separate routes for the S3 API (port 9000) and Console UI (port 9001).
  • Streaming uploads: Allow unlimited request body size and disable request buffering to support uploading objects of any size.
  • Streaming downloads: Disable response buffering to support downloading large objects.

Example configurations

These examples show how to implement the prerequisites for common reverse proxies.

Add these directives to your NGINX server block:

# Allow unlimited upload size
client_max_body_size 0;

# Disable buffering for streaming
proxy_buffering off;
proxy_request_buffering off;

For additional NGINX proxy configuration options, see the NGINX Proxy Module Documentation.

Add these settings to your HAProxy configuration:

defaults
    # Extended timeouts for large operations
    timeout client  300s
    timeout server  300s

HAProxy does not buffer request bodies by default. No directive is needed to stream large uploads, matching the NGINX proxy_request_buffering off setting above.

For additional HAProxy configuration options, see the HAProxy Configuration Manual.

Configuration requirements

Configure HyperVault with the appropriate environment variable and DNS settings to ensure proper communication through your load balancer.

Domain-based routing uses separate hostnames for the S3 API and Console UI (recommended for production deployments).

  1. Configure your load balancer to route traffic based on hostname:

    • hypervault.example.com → Backend port 9000
    • console.hypervault.example.com → Backend port 9001

  2. Set HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL to your Console UI domain:

    HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL="https://console.hypervault.example.com"

    Add this variable to /etc/default/hypervault then restart the HyperVault service:

    sudo systemctl restart hypervault-server

Path-based routing uses a single hostname with different paths for the S3 API and Console UI.

  1. Configure your load balancer to route traffic based on URL path:

    • / (root path) → Backend port 9000 (S3 API)
    • /console → Backend port 9001 (Console UI)

  2. Set HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL to your Console UI path:

    HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL="https://hypervault.example.com/console"

    Add this variable to /etc/default/hypervault then restart the HyperVault service:

    sudo systemctl restart hypervault-server

For detailed information about the HYPERVAULT_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL environment variable and additional console configuration options, see Console Environment Variables.

Verify your configuration

After configuring your load balancer, verify it works correctly using the load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname before updating production DNS.

  1. Test the health endpoint through your load balancer:

    curl https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME/hypervault/health/live

    Expected response: 200 OK with body OK

    Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname.

    For comprehensive health check documentation, see Health Check Probes.

  2. Configure and test the HyperVault Client connection using your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname:

    mc alias set myhypervault https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME ACCESS_KEY SECRET_KEY
mc ping myhypervault
mc ready myhypervault

    Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname, and ACCESS_KEY and SECRET_KEY with appropriate credentials.

  3. Verify Console UI access by opening https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME in your web browser, logging in, and browsing objects.

    Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname.

Update DNS for production

After successfully verifying your load balancer configuration, update your DNS records to point your production endpoints to the load balancer.

Create DNS A or CNAME records pointing to your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname:

  • hypervault.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname (S3 API)
  • console.hypervault.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname (Console UI)

Create a DNS A or CNAME record pointing to your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname:

  • hypervault.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname

Once DNS propagates, clients can access HyperVault through the configured domain names.

Configure your load balancer to route traffic based on hostname: aistor.example.com → Backend port 9000 console.aistor.example.com → Backend port 9001 Set MINIO_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL to your Console UI domain: MINIO_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL="https://console.aistor.example.com" Add this variable to /etc/default/minio then restart the MinIO AIStor service: sudo systemctl restart aistor-server Path-based routing Path-based routing uses a single hostname with different paths for the S3 API and Console UI. Configure your load balancer to route traffic based on URL path: / (root path) → Backend port 9000 (S3 API) /console → Backend port 9001 (Console UI) Set MINIO_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL to your Console UI path: MINIO_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL="https://aistor.example.com/console" Add this variable to /etc/default/minio then restart the MinIO AIStor service: sudo systemctl restart aistor-server For detailed information about the MINIO_BROWSER_REDIRECT_URL environment variable and additional console configuration options, see Console Environment Variables. Verify your configuration After configuring your load balancer, verify it works correctly using the load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname before updating production DNS. Test the health endpoint through your load balancer: curl https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME/minio/health/live Expected response: 200 OK with body OK Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname. For comprehensive health check documentation, see Health Check Probes. Configure and test the AIStor Client connection using your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname: mc alias set myaistor https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME ACCESS_KEY SECRET_KEY mc ping myaistor mc ready myaistor Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname, and ACCESS_KEY and SECRET_KEY with appropriate credentials. Verify Console UI access by opening https://LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME in your web browser, logging in, and browsing objects. Replace LOAD_BALANCER_IP_OR_HOSTNAME with your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname. Update DNS for production After successfully verifying your load balancer configuration, update your DNS records to point your production endpoints to the load balancer. Domain-based routing Create DNS A or CNAME records pointing to your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname: aistor.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname (S3 API) console.aistor.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname (Console UI) Path-based routing Create a DNS A or CNAME record pointing to your load balancer’s client-facing IP or hostname: aistor.example.com → Load balancer IP/hostname Once DNS propagates, clients can access MinIO AIStor through the configured domain names.

title: Enable Network Encryption | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Enable Network Encryption

HyperVault implements Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2+ encryption with support for Server Name Indication (SNI) for selecting relevant TLS certificates in response to client requests.

You must set up TLS before you can enable data encryption, also called server-side encryption. See Configure TLS Network Encryption for how to do it on .deb or .rpm based Linux distributions.

HyperVault supports the following types of certificate signatures:

  • self-signed

  • internal or private certificate authorities (CAs)

  • third-party CAs

Multiple certificates are implemented with SNI to determine which certificate to return to a client based on the hostname in the request.

Certificate path

HyperVault searches for TLS certificates at $HOME/.hypervault/certs by default. The certificate directory must contain a PEM-encoded TLS key pair named public.crt and private.key. PFX (.pfx) certificate bundles are not supported.

If the private.key is password protected, set the HYPERVAULT_CERT_PASSWD environment variable so HyperVault can decrypt it at startup, and ensure the encrypted key uses the PKCS-1 format. See Encrypted private keys for details.

If you install with the binary, this directory is created automatically.

The HyperVault DEB or RPM installers, however, create a hypervault-user system user that has no home directory or login privileges. In this case, follow the instructions to Enable TLS Encryption. These instructions explain manually creating the certificate path.

To use a custom certificate path, specify the --certs-dir flag or set the path in the environment file as part of HYPERVAULT_OPTS:

hypervault server --certs-dir /path/to/custom/certs

Make sure the user running the HyperVault service has read permissions to the certificate files and write permissions to the certificate directory.

Multiple TLS certificates

HyperVault supports multiple TLS certificates for different hostnames using Server Name Indication (SNI). Organize certificates in the following directory structure:

certs/
 ├─ public.crt         # Default certificate
 ├─ private.key        # Default private key
 │
 ├─ example.com/       # Subdirectory name is ignored
 │  ├─ public.crt
 │  └─ private.key
 └─ internal.corp/
    ├─ public.crt
    └─ private.key

Each key pair must use the file names public.crt and private.key. HyperVault ignores the subdirectory names but skips any directory named CAs or prefixed with ... Symbolic links to directories are supported and resolved automatically.

When a client connects, HyperVault uses SNI to match the requested hostname against the Subject Alternative Names (SANs) of the available certificates. HyperVault returns the first certificate whose SAN matches the requested hostname. If no certificate matches, or if the client does not send an SNI hostname (for example, when connecting directly to an IP address), HyperVault returns the default certificate from the root directory.

For detailed instructions, examples of certificate directory structure, and security guidance on certificate placement, see Configure TLS Network Encryption.

Certificate authorities

HyperVault loads trusted CA certificates from both the host system’s root certificate store and the CAs/ subdirectory within the certificate directory (for example, $HOME/.hypervault/certs/CAs/). Place PEM-encoded CA certificate files in this directory. HyperVault reads all top-level files in the CAs/ directory and adds valid X.509 PEM certificates to the trusted root CA pool.

If HyperVault cannot verify an incoming client’s TLS certificate against the combined CA pool, the server rejects the connection.

HyperVault also adds the public certificates from all loaded TLS key pairs to the root CA pool. This allows self-signed certificates to work without placing a copy in the CAs/ directory. For production deployments, place the issuing CA certificate in the CAs/ directory rather than relying on this behavior.

When using certificate-based STS authentication (AssumeRoleWithCertificate), HyperVault allows up to 10 intermediate CA certificates in the client certificate chain.

Automatic certificate reloading

HyperVault automatically reloads TLS certificates when the underlying files change. On Linux, HyperVault uses inotify to watch for IN_CLOSE_WRITE and IN_MOVED_TO events on the certificate directories. On other platforms, HyperVault watches for file Create and Write events. This detects certificate updates made by writing a new file and renaming it into place (atomic update), which is the recommended method for rotating certificates.

When a file change is detected, HyperVault re-reads both public.crt and private.key, computes SHA-256 hashes of the new content, and reloads the certificate only if the content has changed. If the reload fails due to an invalid key pair or a partially written file, HyperVault continues serving the previously loaded certificate.

For certificates that use symbolic links (common with cert-manager on Kubernetes or other automated certificate management tools), HyperVault polls the symlink targets every 10 seconds to detect changes.

Full rescan on SIGHUP

Automatic reloading detects modifications to existing certificate files. To pick up structural changes to the certificates directory, such as adding or removing subdirectories, send the SIGHUP signal to trigger a full rescan.

Use SIGHUP when you:

  • Add new certificate subdirectories for additional hostnames.
  • Remove certificate subdirectories that are no longer needed.
  • Reorganize the certificate directory structure.

To trigger a certificate rescan on a single node:

systemctl reload hypervault

After a certificate renewal that touches every node, trigger the rescan across the entire cluster with clush (or any equivalent parallel-SSH tool):

clush -w @storage-nodes "systemctl reload hypervault"

If systemctl reload hypervault fails with Job type reload is not applicable, the installed hypervault.service predates the ExecReload= directive. Add ExecReload=/bin/kill -SIGHUP $MAINPID to the [Service] section of the unit file and run systemctl daemon-reload.

If certificate loading fails during the rescan, HyperVault continues using the previously loaded certificates.

Internode connections

HyperVault uses a separate configuration for internal, internode connections. When a node sends a request to another node, it includes a hash of the public key derived from the root credentials to establish trust. This requires that nodes have a direct TLS connection to all other nodes in the cluster.

If you require a reverse proxy or similar service between nodes, this may cause TLS to fail. Create an issue in SUBNET for assistance is configuring the system to work in such a scenario.

Recommendations for generating certificates

Supported TLS cipher suites

HyperVault in FIPS mode supports only the AES-GCM ciphers. FIPS mode excludes CHACHA20_POLY1305 and all CBC cipher suites.

Supported X.509 certificate public keys

HyperVault supports the following public key algorithms:

  • RSA-2048 up to RSA-4096, OAEP and PSS
  • ECDSA with P-256, P-384 and P-521
  • EdDSA/Ed25519

HyperVault in FIPS mode does not support EdDSA/Ed25519 algorithms.

Supported X.509 signature hash functions

HyperVault supports the following signature hash functions:

  • SHA2-256
  • SHA2-384
  • SHA2-512

title: Configure TLS Network Encryption | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Configure TLS Network Encryption

This procedure explains how to specify the TLS certificates your HyperVault deployment requires and configure your deployment to work with the certificates. See also Enable Network Encryption for explanations of how HyperVault requires TLS and which cipher suites HyperVault supports.

Prerequisites

  • The appropriate X.509 certificates for your environment.

  • Read and write permissions to the appropriate directories for the user to add certificates.

Procedure

  1. Create the certificates and Certificate Authorities (CAs) your environment requires.

  2. Create the appropriate directories for your certificates and CAs.

    # example certificates path
/opt/hypervault/certs

# example CAs path
/opt/hypervault/certs/CAs

  3. Set the ownership of these directories to hypervault-user:

    sudo chown -R hypervault-user:hypervault-user /opt/hypervault/certs

  4. Add the default certificates to the /certs directory. At least one private.key and public.crt must be placed at the root of the certs directory, to provide the default certificate.

    /certs
  private.key
  public.crt

    If your private.key is password protected, see Encrypted private keys below for the additional configuration required.

  5. (Optional) Add more certificates per domain as your environment requires.

    Create a subdirectory in the /certs directory for the hostname(s) a certificate supports with its DNS or IP Subject Alternative Name (SAN) list. HyperVault ignores subdirectory names in certificate selection, relying solely on SNI matching against the certificate’s SAN list. See Multiple TLS Certificates.

    HyperVault uses the certificate at the root level (/certs/private.key and /certs/public.crt) as the default certificate. HyperVault returns this certificate when the hostname specified by the client does not match any other configured certificates.

    The following directory structure example supports multiple TLS certificates, with a distinct default and hostname-specific certificate directories.

    /certs
  private.key
  public.crt # default certificate for public clients (SANs: *.example.com, example.com)
  /internode # use descriptive subdirectory names; HyperVault relies on the SAN list for selection
    private.key
    public.crt # internal certificate for internode traffic (SANs: node1.internal.com, node2.internal.com, or *.cluster.local)
  /s3.example.net
    private.key
    public.crt # optional additional public certificate for different domain (SANs: *.s3.example.net)
    Certificate Placement and Security
    Place your public-facing certificate (for S3 clients) at the top level to prevent exposing internal certificate details. Putting certificates that expose internal hostnames in the default root certificate directory allows any requesting client to view those hostnames.

  6. (Optional) Add CAs for trusting remote hosts. Place the CA files in the /certs/CAs directory. See Certificate Authorities.

  7. Modify the environment file at /etc/default/hypervault. Open the file and modify the HYPERVAULT_OPTS and HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES values as follows:

    • HYPERVAULT_OPTS - add the certs-dir parameter pointing at the directory you created for storing certificates.

    • HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES - change the http:// protocol to https://.

    HYPERVAULT_OPTS="--certs-dir /opt/hypervault/certs"

# specify https for all nodes
HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="https://..."

  8. Restart HyperVault and monitor the server logs to make sure that all nodes restart and resume operations. You must update your clients to connect to HyperVault with the TLS protocol.

    mc admin service restart

# update the alias with the new hostname
mc alias set https://hypervault.example.net:9000 USERNAME PASSWORD

mc admin info --debug

    The --debug output should show a successful TLS handshake between the client and HyperVault server.

Encrypted private keys

If your private.key is password protected, set the HYPERVAULT_CERT_PASSWD environment variable to the key’s password before starting the server so HyperVault can decrypt the key at startup. Add the variable to the environment file at /etc/default/hypervault or export it in the shell that starts the service:

export HYPERVAULT_CERT_PASSWD=<PASSWORD>

HyperVault supports only PKCS-1 encrypted private keys. The default OpenSSL format for encrypted private keys is PKCS-8, which HyperVault does not support. Convert a PKCS-8 RSA key to PKCS-1 with the following command:

openssl rsa -in private-pkcs8-key.key -aes256 -passout pass:PASSWORD -out private.key

HyperVault supports keys and certificates only in PEM format. PFX (.pfx) certificate bundles are not supported.

Certificate changes

After initial TLS configuration, you can update certificates without restarting the HyperVault service when running HyperVault Server RELEASE.2026-02-02T23-40-11Z or later. On older version of the HyperVault Server, you must restart the server to load the certificate changes.

If you modify or replace an existing certificate in place, HyperVault automatically reloads the modified TLS certificates. For example, when you replace a near-expiration public.crt and private.key key pair with a newer set, HyperVault uses the new certificates automatically.

If you add an entirely new certificate or remove an old one with no replacement, run systemctl reload hypervault to trigger a reload of the certificates directory without fully restarting HyperVault.

The process of adding a new certificate might resemble the following set of commands:

# Add new certificate for additional hostname
mkdir -p /opt/hypervault/certs/api.example.net
cp api.example.net.crt /opt/hypervault/certs/api.example.net/public.crt
cp api.example.net.key /opt/hypervault/certs/api.example.net/private.key

# Signal HyperVault to rescan certificates
systemctl reload hypervault

To trigger the rescan across every node after a cluster-wide renewal, use clush (or any equivalent parallel-SSH tool):

clush -w @storage-nodes "systemctl reload hypervault"

See Certificate reloading for more information.

Troubleshooting

If clients receive the wrong certificate or TLS handshakes fail:

  • Verify the certificate’s Subject Alternative Names (SANs) match the hostname clients are using.
  • Check that certificates are readable by the hypervault-user.
  • Do not rename directories, as directory names do not affect which certificate HyperVault returns.

title: Enable Server Side Encryption | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Enable Server Side Encryption

Server-Side Encryption (SSE) encrypts objects as HyperVault writes them, protecting your data at rest without requiring clients to encrypt data themselves. SSE also underpins regulatory and compliance requirements around secure locking and erasure of data.

To perform SSE, HyperVault Server connects to a key manager that stores and protects the encryption keys. This page introduces how HyperVault encrypts data, how to choose a key manager, and the encryption types HyperVault supports. When you are ready to enable SSE, follow the procedure for your key manager:

  • Server-Side Encryption with HyperVault KMS — recommended for new deployments.
  • Server-Side Encryption with KES — to connect a supported third-party KMS.

How HyperVault encrypts data

HyperVault uses envelope encryption, a layered approach where keys protect other keys:

  • A master key (also called an external key) is a long-lived key stored in the key manager. HyperVault never holds the plaintext master key on disk — it stays in the key manager.

  • For each object, HyperVault requests a unique data key derived from a master key. It encrypts the object with the data key, then stores only an encrypted copy of the data key in the object metadata. To read the object, HyperVault asks the key manager to decrypt the data key, then decrypts the object.

Because the plaintext master keys exist only inside the key manager, controlling access to the key manager controls access to every object it protects. This property is what makes secure erasure and locking possible.

When you enable SSE, HyperVault also encrypts its own backend — identity and access management (IAM) data, configuration, and other internal state — using the default master key.

After you enable SSE, HyperVault requires access to the key manager and the default master key to decrypt the backend and start. You cannot disable or reset backend encryption once enabled.

For a deeper explanation of the key manager itself, see the HyperVault KMS documentation.

Choose a key manager

HyperVault supports three key managers. Configure exactly one through the server-side encryption settings.

Key manager Use it when Learn more
HyperVault KMS (recommended) You want a dedicated root key manager with native HyperVault integration. This is the default key manager for new deployments. Enable with HyperVault KMS
Key Encryption Service (KES) You must store master keys in a supported third-party KMS, such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Entrust, Fortanix, or Thales. Considered legacy. Enable with KES
Static key You are testing or evaluating SSE. Not for production. HYPERVAULT_KMS_SECRET_KEY

HyperVault KMS provides equivalent functionality to third-party KMS solutions for managing root encryption keys. If you run KES today, you can migrate to HyperVault KMS without re-encrypting your data.

Supported encryption types

HyperVault SSE is feature and API compatible with AWS Server-Side Encryption and supports the following encryption strategies:

HyperVault automatically deploys with SSE-KMS encryption of all objects written to a bucket using a specific external key stored in an external key manager. Clients can override the bucket default by specifying an explicit key as part of the write operation.

For buckets without automatic SSE-KMS encryption, clients can specify a key as part of the write operation instead.

You cannot disable SSE-KMS encryption once enabled. HyperVault encrypts backend data as part of enabling server-side encryption.

SSE-KMS provides more granular and customizable encryption compared to SSE-S3 and SSE-C.

HyperVault supports automatic SSE-S3 encryption of all objects written to a bucket with an external key stored in the external key manager. HyperVault SSE-S3 supports one external key for the entire deployment.

For buckets without automatic SSE-S3 encryption, clients can request SSE encryption as part of the write operation instead.

Clients specify an external key as part of the write operation for an object. HyperVault uses the specified key to perform SSE-S3.

SSE-C does not support bucket-default encryption settings and requires clients to perform all key management operations.

SSE-C requires TLS/HTTPS
SSE-C requires a TLS/HTTPS-enabled deployment. The S3 client transmits the customer-provided encryption key in the HTTP request headers, so the key must never travel over plain HTTP.

SSE-C key rotation

S3 clients can change the client-provided key of an existing object. To rotate the key, the client performs an S3 COPY operation where the copy source and destination are the same object, supplying both the current and new keys in the request headers:

Header Value
X-Amz-Server-Side-Encryption-Customer-Key Base64-encoded new key
X-Amz-Copy-Source-Server-Side-Encryption-Customer-Key Base64-encoded current key

Such a self-COPY request is also known as S3 SSE-C key rotation.

Secure erasure and locking

Because HyperVault needs the encryption key — and therefore the key manager — to decrypt an object, you can securely lock or erase objects by controlling access to the key.

General strategies include, but are not limited to:

  • Seal the key manager so HyperVault can no longer reach any keys. This locks all SSE-KMS and SSE-S3 encrypted objects. The objects remain unreadable as long as the key manager stays sealed.

  • Seal or unmount an encryption key. This locks all SSE-KMS or SSE-S3 encrypted objects protected by that key. The objects remain unreadable as long as the key remains sealed.

  • Delete an encryption key. This renders all SSE-KMS or SSE-S3 encrypted objects protected by the key permanently unreadable. Combining key deletion with data deletion may satisfy regulatory requirements for secure erasure.

    Deleting a key is typically irreversible. Exercise extreme caution before intentionally deleting a master key.

SSE also underpins regulatory and compliance requirements around secure locking and erasure of data. To perform SSE, AIStor Server connects to a key manager that stores and protects the encryption keys. This page introduces how AIStor encrypts data, how to choose a key manager, and the encryption types AIStor supports. Server-Side Encryption with KES — to connect a supported third-party KMS. title: Server Side Encryption with HyperVault KMS | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Server Side Encryption with HyperVault KMS

This procedure enables Server-Side Encryption (SSE) on a Linux HyperVault deployment using HyperVault KMS as the key manager. HyperVault KMS is the recommended key manager for new deployments.

For background on how HyperVault encrypts data and the encryption types it supports, see Enable Server-Side Encryption.

Enabling SSE on a HyperVault deployment automatically encrypts the backend data for that deployment using the default encryption key selected during setup.

HyperVault requires access to HyperVault KMS to decrypt the backend and start normally. You can neither disable nor reset encryption of the backend.

Prerequisites

Network encryption (TLS)

HyperVault KMS requires TLS connectivity between client and server to protect cryptographic payloads during transmission.

Review the networking tutorials and enable TLS before proceeding with this tutorial.

Mutual TLS and network path

HyperVault authenticates to HyperVault KMS with mutual TLS (mTLS), where the client presents its own certificate to the server during the TLS handshake. HyperVault derives that client certificate from the HYPERVAULT_KMS_API_KEY value and presents it on every connection. HyperVault KMS identifies the caller from the public key in the certificate. It does not validate the certificate against a certificate authority (CA), so there is no client CA to configure on the HyperVault KMS side.

The client certificate reaches HyperVault KMS only if nothing along the way terminates TLS. Expose HyperVault KMS through a TCP (Layer 4) load balancer or a passthrough listener. Do not place HyperVault KMS behind an HTTP or HTTPS (Layer 7) ingress. A Layer 7 ingress terminates TLS and opens its own connection to HyperVault KMS, so the client certificate never arrives and requests fail with the following message:

client certificate required: client has not sent any certificate during the TLS handshake
A Layer 7 ingress can report HyperVault KMS as healthy while every cryptographic call fails. HyperVault KMS accepts requests without a client certificate on four routes: /version, /v1/health/live, /v1/health/ready, and /v1/health/metrics. Health checks and metrics scrapes therefore succeed, while every request to /v1/kms returns the error above.

HyperVault KMS

This procedure assumes you have an existing HyperVault KMS deployment. See the HyperVault KMS documentation for guidance on installation and configuration.

From that tutorial you need the HyperVault KMS server endpoints and three resources. Create the resources in the order listed, because each one depends on the previous:

  1. An enclave dedicated to this object store. An enclave is an isolated namespace within HyperVault KMS that holds its own keys and identities. Create it with the minkms add-enclave command.

  2. An administrator identity scoped to that enclave, created with the minkms add-identity command and its --admin flag. The command prints an API key once and cannot display it again, so record it before continuing. Do not reuse the HyperVault KMS cluster administrator API key. HyperVault logs a warning at startup if the API key it receives has SysAdmin privileges.

  3. A default SSE key inside that enclave, created with the minkms add-key command.

Each value maps onto one of the environment variables you set later in this procedure:

Value from HyperVault KMS Environment variable
HyperVault KMS server endpoints HYPERVAULT_KMS_SERVER
Enclave name HYPERVAULT_KMS_ENCLAVE
API key of the enclave administrator identity HYPERVAULT_KMS_API_KEY
Default SSE key name HYPERVAULT_KMS_SSE_KEY

Utilities

This procedure uses the base64 and yq utilities. Install both utilities on your local host system.

Procedure

  1. Retrieve and take a backup of the environment file

    Copy the contents of /etc/default/hypervault to a backup file .timestamp.bak before proceeding.

  2. Add HyperVault KMS settings to the environment file

    Open the /etc/default/hypervault file in your preferred text editor and add the following lines:

     # HyperVault KMS settings

 # Provide a list of hostnames associated to your HyperVault KMS deployment. HyperVault server load-balances and fails over across the MinKMS servers natively.
 # Alternatively specify a TCP (Layer 4) load balancer that passes TLS through to the HyperVault KMS hosts.
 # A load balancer or ingress that terminates TLS breaks mutual TLS authentication.

 HYPERVAULT_KMS_SERVER="https://kms-1.example.net,https://kms-2.example.net,https://kms3-example.net"

 # Specify the name for the default encryption key
 # This key is used for backend and default bucket encryption.
 # Consider specifying a unique key name to facilitate easy identification among other stored keys.
 #
 # Do not modify the HYPERVAULT_KMS_SSE_KEY value after setup.
 # HyperVault requires this key to start successfully.

 HYPERVAULT_KMS_SSE_KEY="object-store-primary-default-key"

 # Specify the HyperVault KMS enclave to use

 HYPERVAULT_KMS_ENCLAVE="object-store-primary"

 # Specify the HyperVault KMS API key to use for authenticating operations.
 # The API key must have permission to access and perform operations in the HyperVault KMS enclave

 HYPERVAULT_KMS_API_KEY="k1:APIKEYSTRING"

    Apply this change to all nodes in the HyperVault deployment. The contents of the environment file must match exactly. Use a utility like shasum to ensure checksums match across all files before proceeding.

  3. Restart HyperVault

    Use the mc admin service restart command to restart all HyperVault nodes simultaneously.

    Monitor the nodes for successful startup.

  4. Enable bucket default encryption

    Use the mc CLI tool to connect to the HyperVault deployment. Use the mc encrypt set command to set bucket default encryption.

    For example:

    mc mb object-store/data
mc encrypt set sse-kms object-store/data

    To encrypt a bucket with a dedicated key instead of the default key, create the key with mc admin kms key create first:

    mc admin kms key create object-store data-bucket-encryption-key
mc mb object-store/data
mc encrypt set sse-kms data-bucket-encryption-key object-store/data

    Write a file to the bucket with mc cp or any S3-compatible SDK, then run mc stat on the file to confirm the associated encryption metadata.

title: Server Side Encryption with KES | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Server Side Encryption with KES

This page enables Server-Side Encryption (SSE) on a Linux HyperVault deployment using the Key Encryption Service (KES) to connect a supported third-party KMS. For instructions on running KES, see the KES docs.

For background on how HyperVault encrypts data and the encryption types it supports, see Enable Server-Side Encryption.

KES is legacy
KES is the legacy path for integrating a third-party KMS. New deployments should use HyperVault KMS instead. If you already run KES, you can migrate to HyperVault KMS without re-encrypting your data.

Broadly, the required steps are:

  1. Create a new external key (EK) for server-side encryption (SSE).

  2. Create or modify a HyperVault deployment to support SSE with KES.

  3. Configure automatic bucket-default SSE.

Enabling SSE on a HyperVault deployment automatically encrypts the backend data for that deployment using the default encryption key.

HyperVault requires access to KES and the external KMS to decrypt the backend and start normally. The KMS must maintain access to the HYPERVAULT_KMS_KES_KEY_NAME. Once enabled, you cannot disable or reset encryption of the backend.

Prerequisites

  • HyperVault access with mc configured with an alias

  • An existing KES installation connected to a supported KMS installation, both accessible from the local host. Refer to the installation instructions for your supported KMS target to deploy KES and connect it to a KMS solution:

  • AWS Secrets Manager

  • Azure KeyVault

  • Entrust KeyControl

  • Fortanix SDKMS

  • Google Cloud Secret Manager

  • HashiCorp Vault

  • Thales CipherTrust Manager (formerly Gemalto KeySecure)

Procedure

  1. Generate a KES API key for HyperVault

    Run the kes identity new command to generate a new API key:

    kes identity new

    The output includes both the API key for HyperVault and the identity hash for the KES Policy configuration.

  2. Edit the HyperVault environment file

    Create or modify the environment file for all hosts in the target deployment to include the following environment variables:

    # Add these environment variables to the existing environment file

HYPERVAULT_KMS_KES_ENDPOINT=https://HOSTNAME:7373
HYPERVAULT_KMS_KES_API_KEY="kes:v1:ACTpAsNoaGf2Ow9o5gU8OmcaG6Af/VcZ1Mt7ysuKoBjv"

# Allows validation of the KES Server Certificate (Self-Signed or Third-Party CA)
# Change this path to the location of the KES CA Path
HYPERVAULT_KMS_KES_CAPATH=/opt/kes/certs/kes-server.cert

# Sets the default KMS key for the backend and SSE-KMS/SSE-S3 Operations)
HYPERVAULT_KMS_KES_KEY_NAME=hypervault-backend-default-key

    Replace HOSTNAME with the IP address or hostname of the KES server. If the HyperVault host machines cannot resolve or reach the specified HOSTNAME, the deployment may return errors or fail to start.

    • If using a single KES server host, specify the IP or hostname of the host
    • If using multiple KES server hosts, specify a comma-separated list of IPs or hostnames of each host

    HyperVault uses the HYPERVAULT_KMS_KES_KEY_NAME key for the following cryptographic operations:

    • Encrypting the HyperVault backend (IAM, configuration, etc.)

    • Encrypting objects using SSE-KMS if the request does not include a specific key.

    • Encrypting objects using SSE-S3.

    HyperVault defaults to expecting this file at /etc/default/hypervault. If you modified your deployment to use a different location for the environment file, modify the file at that location.

  3. Start HyperVault

    You can use the mc admin service restart command to restart HyperVault:

    mc admin service restart ALIAS

  4. Generate a New Encryption Key

    HyperVault requires that the key exist on the KMS before performing operations with the key.

    Run kes key create or mc admin kms key create to add a new key.

    The following command runs mc admin kms key create to add a new External Key (EK) stored on the KMS server for use with encrypting the HyperVault backend.

    mc admin kms key create ALIAS KEYNAME

  5. Enable SSE-KMS for a Bucket

    You can use either the console or the HyperVault Client CLI to enable bucket-default SSE-KMS with the generated key:

    1. In the Console UI, create a new bucket. Or, select an existing bucket.

    2. In the left-hand menu, select Encryption, provide the required information, and select Save.

    3. Add a file to the bucket, and confirm the associated encryption metadata.

    The following commands:

    • Create a new bucket for storing encrypted data
    • Enable SSE-KMS encryption on that bucket
    mc mb local/encryptedbucket
mc encrypt set SSE-KMS encrypted-bucket-key ALIAS/encryptedbucket

    Write a file to the bucket with mc cp or any S3-compatible SDK with a PutObject function. You can then run mc stat on the file to confirm the associated encryption metadata.

title: Deploy HyperVault on macOS | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Deploy HyperVault on macOS

HyperVault is licensed under the HyperVault Software License. An active license is required for production deployments.

This section documents steps for installing and managing HyperVault Server on macOS™ host machines.

Procedure

  1. Install HyperVault Server onto the macOS host

    The easiest way to install HyperVault Server on macOS is using Homebrew.

    Alternatively, HyperVault provides binaries for M-series processors (ARM64) and older Intel-based processors (AMD64). Download the binary, set it as executable, and copy it to a location in your $PATH such as /usr/local/bin

    brew install hypervault/hypervault/hypervault

    curl --progress-bar -L https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/darwin-arm64/hypervault -o hypervault
chmod +x ./hypervault
mv ./hypervault /usr/local/bin #may require sudo permissions

hypervault --version

    curl --progress-bar -L https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/darwin-amd64/hypervault -o hypervault
chmod +x ./hypervault
mv ./hypervault /usr/local/bin #may require sudo permissions

hypervault --version

  2. Retrieve your license file

    HyperVault requires a license to run. You can use an existing license, such as one from SUBNET, or you can request a new HyperVault Free Tier license.

title: Enable Network Encryption | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Enable Network Encryption

HyperVault implements Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2+ encryption with support for Server Name Indication (SNI) for selecting relevant TLS certificates in response to client requests.

You must set up TLS before you can enable data encryption, also called server-side encryption.

HyperVault supports the following types of certificate signatures:

  • self-signed

  • internal or private certificate authorities (CAs)

  • third-party CAs

Multiple certificates are implemented with SNI to determine which certificate to return to a client based on the hostname in the request.

This procedure uses the HyperVault certgen tool to generate self-signed certificates for local testing and development purposes.

Certificate path

HyperVault searches by default for certificates at ~/.hypervault/certs. When HyperVault detects public.crt and private.key files in this directory, it automatically enables TLS.

If the private.key is password protected, set the HYPERVAULT_CERT_PASSWD environment variable so HyperVault can decrypt it at startup, and ensure the encrypted key uses the PKCS-1 format. See Encrypted private keys for the key conversion procedure.

If you work with a user-specified path, use the --certs-dir flag:

hypervault server --certs-dir /path/to/custom/certs /data

Prerequisites

  • The certgen tool for generating self-signed certificates.
  • Alternatively, TLS certificates from your organization’s certificate authority.

Procedure

This procedure assumes you have

  • previously completed the Install HyperVault procedure.
  • have the necessary directories with full write access.
  • have a valid HyperVault License, such as the HyperVault Free license.

1. Generate TLS certificates

Use certgen to generate self-signed TLS certificates for testing and development. For production environments, use certificates issued by a trusted certificate authority.

Install certgen

Download the certgen binary for your Mac.

curl -L https://github.com/hypervault/certgen/releases/latest/download/certgen-darwin-arm64 -o certgen
chmod +x certgen
sudo mv certgen /usr/local/bin/

curl -L https://github.com/hypervault/certgen/releases/latest/download/certgen-darwin-amd64 -o certgen
chmod +x certgen
sudo mv certgen /usr/local/bin/

Generate certificates

Generate a certificate that includes the hostnames and IP addresses clients use to connect to HyperVault.

mkdir -p ~/.hypervault/certs
cd ~/.hypervault/certs
certgen -host "127.0.0.1,localhost"

This creates public.crt and private.key files in the ~/.hypervault/certs directory.

For additional hostnames or IP addresses, include them as a comma-separated list:

certgen -host "127.0.0.1,localhost,hypervault.example.com,192.168.1.100"

2. Run HyperVault with TLS

HyperVault automatically enables TLS when it detects public.crt and private.key files in the ~/.hypervault/certs directory.

hypervault server /tmp/hypervault --license ~/hypervault/hypervault.license

The output indicates TLS is enabled when the URLs use https://:

HyperVault Enterprise Object Store
API: https://192.168.86.35:9000  https://127.0.0.1:9000
   RootUser: hypervaultadmin
   RootPass: hypervaultadmin

WebUI: https://192.168.86.35:9001 https://127.0.0.1:9001
   RootUser: hypervaultadmin
   RootPass: hypervaultadmin

3. Trust additional certificate authorities

If you need HyperVault to trust certificates from additional certificate authorities, such as when connecting to HyperVault KMS with self-signed certificates, place the CA certificates in the ~/.hypervault/certs/CAs directory.

mkdir -p ~/.hypervault/certs/CAs
cp /path/to/ca-certificate.crt ~/.hypervault/certs/CAs/

4. Connect using HTTPS

When TLS is enabled, use https:// instead of http:// when connecting to HyperVault.

Configure mc to trust the certificate

The mc client must trust the HyperVault server’s certificate. The self-signed certificate generated by certgen acts as both the certificate and Certificate Authority (CA). Copy the certificate to the mc configuration directory:

mkdir -p ~/.mc/certs/CAs
cp ~/.hypervault/certs/public.crt ~/.mc/certs/CAs/

Then create an alias using HTTPS:

mc alias set myhypervault https://localhost:9000 hypervaultadmin hypervaultadmin

Alternatively, use the --insecure flag to skip certificate verification (not recommended for production):

mc alias set myhypervault https://localhost:9000 hypervaultadmin hypervaultadmin --insecure

Access the Console

Open your browser to https://localhost:9001 to access the Console.

When using self-signed certificates, your browser displays a security warning. You can proceed by accepting the certificate or add it to your system’s trusted certificates.

Recommendations for generating certificates

Supported TLS cipher suites

title: Deploy HyperVault Server on Windows | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Deploy HyperVault Server on Windows

HyperVault is licensed under the HyperVault Software License. An active license is required for production deployments.

This procedure downloads and installs the HyperVault Server onto a host running Microsoft Windows Server or Windows 11 Professional Edition.

Review the Hardware and System Requirements to ensure your target infrastructure meets our guidance.

Procedure

  1. Download the HyperVault Server binary 

    Invoke-WebRequest https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/windows-amd64/hypervault -OutFile C:\hypervault.exe

  2. Create a data directory for use with the server

    The following example uses the path $HOME/hypervault/data. Changes this path to reflect the folder, storage volume, or drive intended for use with the server.

    md C:\hypervault

  3. Retrieve your license file

    HyperVault requires a license to run. You can use an existing license, such as one from SUBNET, or you can request a new HyperVault Free Tier license.

    To request a new HyperVault Free Tier license, go to the HyperVault pricing page and select Get Started under the Free tier to obtain a free license. The free tier license allows you to run HyperVault on a single compute resource with one or more drives.

    Download the license file to C:\hypervault\hypervault.license for use in later steps.

    Free tier licenses do not include support. For support options, see the HyperVault pricing page. For more information about licenses, see Licenses.

  4. (Optional) Set up TLS

    If you need TLS for your deployment, configure it before starting the server. See Set up network encryption for instructions.

  5. Run the server process 

    hypervault.exe server C:\hypervault --license C:\hypervault\hypervault.license

    The output of the command includes the startup message from the HyperVault Server. To access the server, use the localhost or 127.0.0.1 address on your local host machine.

  6. Install the HyperVault Client (mc) 

    Invoke-WebRequest https://dl.min.io/hypervault/mc/release/windows-amd64/mc.exe -OutFile C:\mc.exe
C:\mc.exe --version

  7. Connect to the Deployment

    You can connect to the deployment using the built-in Console UI or the HyperVault Client (mc).

    Open your browser to the hostname and port of any node in the deployment. The WebUI output from the previous step indicates which hostnames and ports the hypervault process listens on.

    Log in using the default hypervaultadmin:hypervaultadmin username and password.

    1. Create a new alias for the HyperVault server:

      mc.exe alias set myhypervault http://localhost:9000

      Replace the URL with the hostname of any node in the deployment or a load balancer, reverse proxy, or similar network control plane component managing connections to the deployment.

    2. Create a bucket and copy a file to that bucket:

      mc.exe mb myhypervault/data
mc.exe cp C:\somefile.txt myhypervault/data

Copy the certificate to the mc configuration directory: md $env:USERPROFILE\.mc\certs\CAs copy C:\minio\certs\public.crt $env:USERPROFILE\.mc\certs\CAs\ Then create an alias using HTTPS: C:\mc.exe alias set myaistor https://localhost:9000 minioadmin minioadmin Alternatively, use the --insecure flag to skip certificate verification (not recommended for production): C:\mc.exe alias set myaistor https://localhost:9000 minioadmin minioadmin --insecure Access the Console Open your browser to https://localhost:9001 to access the Console. When using self-signed certificates, your browser displays a security warning. You can proceed by accepting the certificate or add it to your system’s trusted certificates. Recommendations for generating certificates Supported TLS cipher suites

title: Operations | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Operations

Operate and maintain HyperVault in production. These pages cover Day 2 and ongoing tasks, including monitoring, scaling, and troubleshooting.

Performance and troubleshooting

Optimize your deployment with performance tuning guidelines for CPU, memory, storage, and network. Validate your configuration with benchmarking tools. Test the layers underneath with network performance testing. Run it before and after an upgrade to establish a baseline, so you can tell a regression from a bad fabric. On an InfiniBand or RoCE fabric, RDMA acceleration moves object data and erasure-coded shards without passing through the kernel network stack. When issues arise, use the debugging and troubleshooting guide for HTTP tracing, diagnostics, and metadata inspection. When a deployment reports more drive usage than its buckets account for, system path growth names each transient .hypervault.sys path, the sweeper responsible for it, and how to reclaim it.

Core concepts

Core concepts explain the foundational technologies that underpin HyperVault. Erasure coding and healing cover how the cluster stores data and repairs itself. AI Workloads covers which of those mechanisms a training or inference pipeline actually touches.

Monitoring and observability

HyperVault provides comprehensive monitoring capabilities to maintain reliability and performance. Use metrics, logging, audit trails, and healthcheck endpoints to track deployment health and identify performance bottlenecks.

For what a bucket actually holds, bucket inventory reports produce scheduled listings of objects and their metadata. Reports are written as CSV, JSON, or Parquet, and can be filtered by prefix, age, size, name pattern, tags, or custom metadata.

Scaling and maintenance

As storage needs grow or change, you can scale your HyperVault deployment by adding server pools to expand capacity or decommissioning pools to remove aging hardware.

For planned maintenance tasks, node maintenance tools allow you to gracefully take nodes offline without disrupting cluster operations. Cordon nodes before hardware maintenance, OS updates, or rolling upgrades.

Failure and recovery

HyperVault includes tools to help you be ready in the event of hardware and software failures. The failure and recovery documentation covers handling drive failures, node failures, and disaster recovery scenarios.

Licensing

HyperVault requires valid enterprise licenses. The license management documentation covers the registration and renewal of the HyperVault Software License used by HyperVault.

Security

Manage the TLS certificates that protect traffic to the deployment with network encryption. It covers provisioning through cert-manager, rotation on Linux and Kubernetes, and diagnosing trust chain errors.

Use batch key rotation to rotate encryption keys without disrupting ongoing operations.

Protect the data directories themselves with storage hardening, which uses SELinux or eBPF LSM to stop an administrator’s rm -rf from reaching drives the HyperVault process manages.

Releases

Each HyperVault release publishes release artifacts including SBOMs in CycloneDX and SPDX formats, Go module listings, and release notes. Use the REST API and RSS/JSON feeds to integrate release monitoring into existing automation pipelines. Production environments that require targeted patches without a full upgrade can request hotfix releases.

The software lifecycle policy defines end-of-life terms, the operating systems and architectures HyperVault runs on, the S3 API surface it implements, and the client SDKs HyperVault maintains.

title: Batch Key Rotation | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Batch Key Rotation

The HyperVault Batch Framework allows you to create, manage, monitor, and execute jobs using a YAML-formatted job definition file (a “batch file”). Batch jobs run directly on the HyperVault deployment to take advantage of the server-side processing power without constraints of the local machine where you run the HyperVault Client.

The keyrotate batch job type performs the following operations on objects in a HyperVault deployment:

  • Encrypts plaintext (unencrypted) objects using SSE-KMS.
  • Rotates encryption keys for objects already encrypted with SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS using SSE-KMS.
  • Rotates encryption keys for internal HyperVault subsystems (IAM configuration, server configuration, tier configuration, and bucket metadata).

The YAML configuration supports filters to restrict key rotation to a specific set of objects by creation date, tags, metadata, KMS key, or encryption status. You can also define retry attempts or set a notification endpoint and token.

Encryption behavior

The batch key rotation job processes objects according to the following rules:

Source Object Type Result
Plaintext (unencrypted) Encrypted with SSE-KMS using the default KMS key
SSE-KMS encrypted Keys rotated with the current default KMS key
SSE-S3 encrypted Converted to SSE-KMS encryption
SSE-C encrypted Skipped (not supported)

To rotate the KMS master key that protects SSE-S3 encrypted objects without converting to SSE-KMS, use mc admin kms key.

Object lock and legal hold

Objects protected by Object Lock or legal hold have special handling:

  • Plaintext objects with lock or legal hold:

    Always skipped. These objects are protected from modification and cannot be encrypted.

  • Encrypted objects with lock or legal hold:

    Skipped by default. Set forceEncryptLocked: true in the job configuration to allow key rotation on these objects.

Internal subsystem encryption

When the batch job uses the cluster’s default KMS key (HYPERVAULT_KMS_SSE_KEY for HyperVault KMS, or HYPERVAULT_KMS_KES_KEY_NAME for KES), the job also re-encrypts internal HyperVault subsystem data on HyperVault Server RELEASE.2026-02-02T23-40-11Z and later:

  • IAM configuration, including users, groups, policies, service accounts, and STS credentials
  • Server configuration and configuration history
  • Tier configuration
  • Bucket metadata, including replication target credentials

Re-encryption with the rotated key ensures all sensitive internal data uses the most current KMS key.

Batch key rotation on any other KMS key(s) has no effect on internal subsystem encryption.

During internal subsystem key rotation, individual internal objects larger than 1 GiB are skipped to prevent memory issues, since these objects are loaded fully into memory for re-encryption. A skipped object surfaces an error in the audit log similar to the following:

object config/large-file size 1073741825 exceeds maximum allowed size 1073741824 for internal rotation

This limit applies only to internal config objects and does not affect rotation of regular object data.

Key rotate batch job reference

Encryption fields

Field Description
key: Optional

The KMS key ID to use for encryption. Defaults to the default KMS key configured for the deployment. Must match the default KMS key.
context: Optional

A base64-encoded JSON object specifying the KMS encryption context. If specified when creating objects, the same context is required to read those objects.

Filter fields

Key rotation batch jobs have no required filter fields. If you do not specify any filters, the job processes all objects in the specified bucket and prefix. When you specify multiple filters, an object must match all specified filter categories to be processed (AND logic between filter types). Within the tags: and metadata: fields, an object matches if any of the specified entries match (OR logic within each field).

Field Description
newerThan: A string representing a length of time in #d#h#s format. Process only objects newer than the specified duration. For example, 7d, 24h, 5d12h30s.
olderThan: A string representing a length of time in #d#h#s format. Process only objects older than the specified duration.
createdAfter: A date in YYYY-MM-DD format. Process only objects created after the specified date.
createdBefore: A date in YYYY-MM-DD format. Process only objects created before the specified date.
tags: Process only objects with tags that match the specified key: and value:. Supports wildcard patterns.
metadata: Process only objects with metadata that match the specified key: and value:. Supports wildcard patterns.
kmskey: Process only objects encrypted with the specified KMS key ID. Applicable only for SSE-KMS encrypted objects.
plaintextOnly: When set to true, process only plaintext (unencrypted) objects. Skip objects that are already encrypted. Default: false (process both plaintext and encrypted objects).
forceEncryptLocked: When set to true, allow key rotation on encrypted objects that have legal hold or object lock. Default: false (skip locked encrypted objects). Plaintext objects with lock are always skipped regardless of this setting.

Notification fields

Use these fields to send a webhook notification when the job completes. The endpoint receives a JSON POST with job results including job ID, start time, completion status, object counts, and bytes transferred.

Field Description
endpoint: The endpoint URL to send job status event notifications.
token: An optional JSON Web Token (JWT) for authentication with the notification endpoint.

Retry fields

If something interrupts the job, you can define a maximum number of retry attempts and how long to wait between retry attempts.

Field Description
attempts: Number of retry attempts before the job fails. If not specified, defaults to 3 attempts.
delay: The minimum time to wait between retry attempts. If not specified, HyperVault waits 25ms between retry attempts.

Sample YAML description file for a keyrotate job type

Use mc batch generate to create a basic keyrotate batch job for further customization:

keyrotate:
  apiVersion: v1
  bucket: BUCKET
  prefix: PREFIX
  encryption:
    key: <kms-key-id> # optional, defaults to the default KMS key
    context: <base64-encoded-kms-context> # optional KMS encryption context

  # optional flags based filtering criteria
  # for all objects
  flags:
    filter:
      newerThan: "7d" # match objects newer than this value (e.g. 7d10h31s)
      olderThan: "7d" # match objects older than this value (e.g. 7d10h31s)
      createdAfter: "date" # match objects created after "date"
      createdBefore: "date" # match objects created before "date"
      tags:
        - key: "name"
          value: "pick*" # match objects with tag 'name', with all values starting with 'pick'
      metadata:
        - key: "content-type"
          value: "image/*" # match objects with 'content-type', with all values starting with 'image/'
      kmskey: "key-id" # match objects encrypted with this KMS key-id
      plaintextOnly: false # set to true to only process unencrypted objects
      forceEncryptLocked: false # set to true to rotate keys on locked encrypted objects
    notify:
      endpoint: "https://notify.endpoint" # notification endpoint to receive job status events
      token: "Bearer xxxxx" # optional authentication token for the notification endpoint
    retry:
      attempts: 10 # number of retries for the job before giving up
      delay: "500ms" # least amount of delay between each retry

Examples

Encrypt all plaintext objects after adding KMS

If you added KMS to an existing deployment and want to encrypt all previously uploaded plaintext objects:

keyrotate:
  apiVersion: v1
  bucket: my-bucket
  encryption: {}  # uses default KMS key
  flags:
    filter:
      plaintextOnly: true  # only encrypt unencrypted objects

Rotate keys for all encrypted objects

To rotate encryption keys for all objects encrypted with the specified kmskey without affecting plaintext objects:

keyrotate:
  apiVersion: v1
  bucket: my-bucket
  encryption: {}
  flags:
    filter:
      kmskey: "old-key-id"  # only rotate objects encrypted with this key

Objects encrypted with another kmskey are left unchanged.

Encrypt and rotate keys for all objects

To encrypt all plaintext objects and rotate keys for all encrypted objects in a single job:

keyrotate:
  apiVersion: v1
  bucket: my-bucket
  encryption: {}  # uses default KMS key
  # no plaintextOnly filter means the job processes both plaintext and encrypted objects

title: Benchmarking | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Benchmarking

HyperVault includes built-in performance testing tools to measure object operations, drive I/O, network bandwidth, site replication throughput, and client-to-server bandwidth.

For OS-level tuning recommendations, see Performance Tuning.

mc support perf

The mc support perf command runs performance tests against a HyperVault deployment.

Run all performance tests:

mc support perf ALIAS

Run a specific test type:

mc support perf [object|drive|net|site-replication|client] ALIAS

Common flags

Flag Description Default
--size Object size for uploads and downloads 64 MiB
--verbose Display per-server statistics false
--duration Maximum duration for each test 10s
--concurrent Concurrent requests per server 32
--airgap Save results locally instead of uploading false

Object performance test

Tests S3 PUT and GET throughput across the cluster:

mc support perf object ALIAS

Example output:

HyperVault 2024.01.01, 4 servers, 16 drives, 64MiB objects, 32 threads
PUT: 2.5 GiB/s, 40 objs/s
GET: 3.2 GiB/s, 51 objs/s

Use --verbose to see per-server breakdown:

mc support perf object ALIAS --verbose

Expected results:

  • Throughput scales linearly with server count.
  • GET is typically 20-30% faster than PUT.
  • Consistent per-server numbers indicate balanced load.

Drive performance test

Tests raw disk I/O performance on each drive:

mc support perf drive ALIAS

Additional flags for the drive test:

Flag Description Default
--filesize Total data per drive 1 GiB
--blocksize Read/write block size 4 MiB
--serial Test drives one-by-one false

Troubleshoot slow drives:

  1. Check for failing drives: mc admin drive info ALIAS
  2. Verify storage configuration.
  3. Check for thermal throttling.
  4. Review filesystem fragmentation.

Network performance test

Tests inter-node network bandwidth. Requires multiple servers in the cluster.

mc support perf net ALIAS

Results should approach physical network capacity. Troubleshoot network issues:

  1. Check switch configuration.
  2. Verify MTU settings (jumbo frames if supported).
  3. Check for packet loss: ping -c 100 -s 1472 <node>
  4. Review network interface errors with ethtool -S.

Site replication performance test

Tests cross-site replication bandwidth for multi-site deployments:

mc support perf site-replication ALIAS

Client performance test

Tests bandwidth from the mc client to the HyperVault cluster:

mc support perf client ALIAS

Saving results

Airgapped mode

Save results locally instead of uploading to SUBNET:

mc support perf ALIAS --airgap

Output is saved to ALIAS-perf_YYYYMMDDHHMMSS.zip.

JSON output

Get results in JSON format for programmatic consumption:

mc support perf ALIAS --json

Best practices

When to benchmark

  1. Initial deployment: Establish baseline performance.
  2. Hardware changes: After adding or replacing drives or nodes.
  3. Configuration changes: After tuning parameters.
  4. Troubleshooting: When investigating performance issues.
  5. Capacity planning: Before adding workload.

Benchmark conditions

For consistent results:

  1. Run during low-traffic periods.
  2. Ensure cluster is healthy: mc admin info ALIAS
  3. Run multiple iterations.
  4. Test with representative object sizes.
  5. Document system configuration.

Tracking results over time

Date Object PUT Object GET Drive R/W Network
2024-01-01 2.5 GiB/s 3.2 GiB/s 1.1 GiB/s 9.5 Gb
2024-02-01 2.4 GiB/s 3.1 GiB/s 1.1 GiB/s 9.4 Gb
2024-03-01 2.0 GiB/s 2.8 GiB/s 0.8 GiB/s 9.5 Gb

A significant drop (greater than 10%) warrants investigation.

Warp benchmarking tool

For detailed S3 benchmarking, use warp:

go install github.com/hypervault/warp@latest

warp mixed --host=server1:9000,server2:9000 \
  --access-key=hypervaultadmin --secret-key=hypervaultadmin

Warp provides:

  • Detailed latency percentiles
  • Mixed workload simulation
  • Configurable object size distributions
  • Multi-client coordination

Published results

Two published tests measure HyperVault above 200 GiB/s of GET throughput on an eight-node cluster. Each reports a different statistic, so the figures below name which.

268 GiB/s peak GET, 120 GiB/s peak PUT — Solidigm, HyperVault, and Intel, against roughly 24 PB raw across 8 nodes with 2 × 400G NICs each, using HyperVault Warp with 256 MiB objects [1]. Sixteen phases ran without an error. These are pure TCP numbers. Results for RDMA acceleration will be published separately.

229 GiB/s average GET, 118 GiB/s average PUT — Supermicro, Intel, and HyperVault, against 8 nodes with 2 × 400GbE each on a non-blocking 400G fabric, using HyperVault Warp with 64 MiB objects at 4096 concurrent requests [2]. Its peak seconds reached 237 and 126 GiB/s.

Each figure describes one cluster. Drives, object size, network, and client count all move the result, so read these to sanity-check your own numbers rather than to predict them.

References

[1] Solidigm, HyperVault, and Intel, “The New Economics of AI Factory Efficiency: Solidigm, HyperVault and Intel Put Object Storage Scaling to the Test.” [Online]. Available: https://www.solidigm.com/content/dam/solidigm/en/site/products/technology/2026/new-economics-of-ai-factory-hypervault/document/new-economics-of-ai-factory-graph.pdf

[2] Supermicro, Intel, and HyperVault, “Supermicro HyperVault Storage Solution Based on Single-Socket X14 Hyper Systems with Intel Xeon Processors: Deliver High Performance Object Storage for AI Data Flow,” Solution Brief, Jul. 2026. [Online]. Available: https://www.supermicro.com/solutions/Solution_Brief_HyperVault_Intel.pdf

title: Core Concepts | HyperVault DocumentationEight hosts make one server poolA load balancer in front of eight nodesOne endpoint, several API surfacesA deployment with two server pools
html:
Core Concepts

A production HyperVault Server deployment consists of at least 8 hosts with homogeneous storage and compute resources.

These hosts make up a server pool, where the HyperVault Server presents the aggregated compute, memory, and storage as a single resource to clients. Each pool consists of one or more erasure sets.

To limit the impact of localized failures in Kubernetes deployments, configure spread zones so that HyperVault distributes Pods across separate failure domains, such as racks or availability zones.

Each HyperVault Server has a complete picture of the distributed topology, such that an application can connect and direct operations against any node in the deployment.

Applications typically should not manage those connections, because any change to the deployment topology would then require an application update. Production deployments should instead use a load balancer, or a similar network control plane component, to manage connections to the HyperVault Server deployment.

Client applications can use any S3-compatible SDK or library to interact with the HyperVault Server deployment.

HyperVault provides SDKs for Go, Python, Java, .NET, and more. They cover the S3 API, and the Go, C++, Rust, and Python SDKs also implement S3 over RDMA.

The same deployment answers more than the S3 API.

  • HyperVault Tables serves an Apache Iceberg REST catalog from the object store itself, with no separate catalog service or metadata database to run.
  • S3 over RDMA reads an object straight into GPU memory over the RDMA fabric, so the payload never passes through the kernel network stack.
  • FTP, FTPS, and SFTP give file clients access to the same buckets, without an export or a gateway in front.

For how these surfaces and the controls around them serve a training or inference pipeline, see AI Workloads. For how the cluster stores data and repairs itself, see Erasure Coding and Healing.

You can expand an HyperVault Server’s available storage through pool expansion.

Each pool consists of an independent group of nodes with their own erasure sets. Adding new pools requires updating all nodes in the deployment with the new topology. In a multi-pool cluster, the receiving HyperVault Server node determines which pool to route a given request to.

Pool expansion requires updating any load balancers or similar network control plane components with the new hostname layout to ensure even distribution of load across nodes.
