title: AI Workloads | HyperVault DocumentationThe same GetObject over TCP and over RDMA
html:
AI Workloads

An AI pipeline reaches the object store in a handful of specific ways. It reads training data, queries structured data as tables, writes checkpoints, and shares the cluster with other jobs doing the same. This page explains which HyperVault mechanism serves each of those, how it works, and what it requires.

HyperVault stores the data. It does not train models or run inference. The mechanisms below are about getting bytes to and from the accelerators that do.

Reading data at pipeline speed

S3 over RDMA removes one copy from the read path. Training and inference jobs read large objects continuously, and at that rate the copy into the application’s memory becomes the limit rather than the storage. The client registers a buffer and sends its descriptor with the request, and the server transfers the object through that buffer directly. The payload never passes through the kernel network stack.

Three operations have an RDMA path: GetObject, PutObject, and UploadPart. Every other operation uses HTTP, whatever the request headers say.

RDMA requires a deployment running the RDMA build of HyperVault Server, an RDMA-capable NIC on the client, and a RoCE v2 or InfiniBand fabric between them. Reading into GPU memory also needs an NVIDIA GPU with GPU-to-NIC peer-to-peer DMA. Your application allocates a buffer, registers it, and the transfer targets that buffer. A GPU training node registers device memory. A CPU inference node registers host memory. Both take the same path at the same speed, so a fleet can mix them without a second configuration. Against a standard deployment, an RDMA request is declined and the client falls back to HTTP.

RDMA runs on two independent paths, and the one above is only the first. S3 over RDMA carries object data between the server and a buffer the client registered, in GPU memory or in host memory. Inter-node RDMA carries erasure-coded shards between HyperVault nodes, needs an RDMA fabric but no GPU, and is enabled separately. See RDMA acceleration for both paths and the fabric requirements.

Querying structured data as tables

Feature tables, labels, and run metadata are usually tabular, and a pipeline queries them rather than reading them whole. HyperVault Tables serves an Apache Iceberg REST catalog from the object store itself. There is no separate catalog service or metadata database to run alongside it.

Query engines connect to that catalog directly. See Connecting query engines to HyperVault Tables for the supported engines and their catalog configurations.

Creating a warehouse also creates a bucket to hold the table data and metadata. You manage the contents of that bucket through the Tables API or the mc table commands, not through general S3 operations. That protects the integrity of the objects underneath.

Sharing a cluster between workloads

Training, evaluation, and serving jobs on one cluster compete for the same request budget. Bucket-level Quality of Service bounds what any one of them can take.

QoS has two enforcement layers. Inside the server, API QoS caps requests per second and concurrent operations per bucket. In front of the server, network QoS caps bandwidth. It is the only layer that can, because bandwidth has to be shaped before the request body is accepted or the response starts streaming.

Two other controls work alongside it. Bucket quotas bound how much data a bucket holds. The scanner evaluates them periodically rather than in real time, so a bucket can pass its quota between cycles. The multi-tenancy guidance covers isolating teams with IAM policies scoped to buckets or prefixes.

Reproducing a run’s inputs

A result is only reproducible if you can still read the exact bytes the run read. On a versioned bucket, every write creates a new version with its own version ID. A read that names a version ID returns that version rather than the latest. Record the version IDs a run consumed. Those inputs stay readable only while the versions themselves are retained. When a rerun has to see the same bytes, exclude those versions from lifecycle expiration or lock them.

When a dataset has to survive deletion attempts as well as overwrites, object locking and immutability enforces Write-Once Read-Many protection on versioned objects. A GOVERNANCE or COMPLIANCE retention mode protects an object for a fixed period. A legal hold protects it indefinitely.

Finding what a bucket holds

Pipelines that build a manifest before a run need to know what a bucket contains without walking it themselves. Bucket inventory reports produce that listing on a schedule. Each report carries object metadata such as size, last modified date, storage class, encryption status, tags, and user metadata.

Reports are written as CSV, JSON, or Parquet, and can be filtered by prefix, age, size, name pattern, tags, or custom metadata. A pipeline reads the report as a file and treats it as the dataset manifest.

Retiring checkpoints

Checkpoints accumulate faster than anything else a training job writes. Object Lifecycle Management expires objects after a set period or after a set number of versions. A checkpoint prefix stays bounded without a cleanup job of your own.

Reaching the data from file-based tools

Data preparation often involves tools that read and write files rather than call an S3 API. Those tools reach the same buckets over SFTP, FTPS, or FTP. They authenticate against the same identity providers and policies as any S3 client.

File access has narrower semantics than the S3 API. Clients see only the latest version of an object, and append and rename are not supported.

title: Erasure Coding | HyperVault DocumentationAn erasure set spans every node in the poolParity is configurable up to half the erasure setShard distribution across an erasure setRead quorumWrite quorumLosing write quorum but keeping read quorumHealing rebuilds the shards that were lost
html:
Erasure Coding

HyperVault Server uses erasure coding to provide data redundancy and availability.

The diagrams and content in this section present a simplified view of erasure coding operations. They do not represent the full complexity of the HyperVault Server erasure coding implementation.

HyperVault groups the drives in each server pool into one or more erasure sets of the same size. By default, each erasure set can contain 2 to 16 drives. On HyperVault Server RELEASE.2026-02-02T23-40-11Z or later, you can configure erasure sets of up to 32 drives with the HYPERVAULT_ERASURE_SET_DRIVE_COUNT environment variable.

HyperVault determines the optimal number and size of erasure sets when it initializes a server pool. You cannot change these settings afterward.

For each write operation, HyperVault partitions the object into data and parity shards.

Data shards contain a portion of a given object. Parity shards contain a mathematical representation of the object used for rebuilding Data shards.

Use mc admin object info to output a summary of a specific object’s shards (also called “parts”) on disk.

Erasure set stripe size sets the maximum possible parity of the deployment. The formula for determining the number of data and parity shards to generate is:

N (ERASURE SET SIZE) = K (DATA) + M (PARITY)

You can set the parity value between 0 and 1/2 the erasure set size.

Production deployments must use a parity of EC:3 or higher. Lower parity values — including the automatic defaults selected for erasure sets of five or fewer drives — do not provide sufficient failure tolerance for production workloads and are suitable for development and testing environments only. With fewer than three parity shards, routine events such as a drive replacement or node maintenance leave at most one shard of remaining tolerance in the affected erasure set.

Objects written with given parity settings do not update automatically if you change the parity values later.

HyperVault requires a minimum of K shards of any type to read an object.

The value K here is the read quorum for the deployment. The erasure set must therefore have at least K healthy drives to support read operations.

HyperVault cannot reconstruct an object that has lost read quorum. You may be able to recover such objects through other means, such as replication resynchronization.

HyperVault requires a minimum of K erasure set drives to write an object.

The value K here is the write quorum for the deployment. The erasure set must therefore have at least K drives online to support write operations. When parity EC:M is exactly 1/2 the erasure set size, the write quorum is K+1 instead, as described below.

HyperVault always attempts to write all N shards across every drive in the erasure set, not just K.

K is a success threshold, not the number of drives HyperVault writes to. For each PUT, HyperVault:

  1. Generates all N shards for the object — K data shards plus M parity shards.
  2. Dispatches every shard in parallel to its corresponding drive in the erasure set.
  3. Waits for a response from every drive, including any drives that fail or time out.
  4. Returns success to the client only after at least K drives (or K+1 when M is exactly half the erasure set, see below) acknowledge a successful write. Otherwise, returns failure.

For example, a 16-drive erasure set with EC:4 parity always attempts 16 individual drive writes per PUT and tolerates up to 4 unsuccessful writes per object before HyperVault returns an error to the client. A 12-drive erasure set with EC:3 parity attempts 12 drive writes and requires at least 9 to succeed.

If parity EC:M is exactly 1/2 the erasure set size, write quorum is K+1.

This prevents a split-brain type scenario, such as one where a network issue isolates exactly half the erasure set drives from the other.

The K+1 logic ensures that a client cannot write the same object twice, once to each half of the erasure set.

When an erasure set loses write quorum but maintains read quorum, HyperVault continues to serve read operations while rejecting write operations until sufficient drives come back online to restore write quorum.

When drives are offline at the time of a PUT, HyperVault automatically upgrades parity by default.

For each drive that is offline at the time of write, HyperVault increases the object’s parity by one and records the upgraded parity in the object’s metadata. For example, on a 16-drive erasure set with EC:4 parity where 2 drives are offline, HyperVault writes the object as EC:6. This ensures that objects written during a partial outage retain the same level of protection as objects written to a fully healthy erasure set. HyperVault bounds what these upgrades can permanently cost with the HYPERVAULT_ERASURE_PARITY_UPGRADE_BUDGET setting, which defaults to 1% of an erasure set’s capacity per outage.

You can change this behavior with the HYPERVAULT_ERASURE_PARITY_FAILURE setting. See Parity retention optimization for capacity planning considerations and the trade-off against the ignore mode.

For an object maintaining read quorum, HyperVault can use any data or parity shard to heal damaged shards.

Use the HyperVault Erasure Coding Calculator to explore the possible erasure set size and distributions for your planned topology. Where possible, use an even number of nodes and an even number of drives per node. This makes topology planning and drive distribution across erasure sets easier to reason about.

Distributing erasure sets across failure domains

For Kubernetes deployments, you can configure spread zones so that object data and parity shards spread across separate physical or logical failure domains, such as racks or availability zones. This strategy lowers the risk of one failure affecting multiple shards of the same erasure set.

When you configure spread zones, the Operator distributes pods across labeled nodes in a round-robin fashion. For example, with a 16-drive erasure set configured with EC:4 parity and 4 availability zones, the Operator ensures that each zone contains drives from the erasure set, providing protection against zone-level failures.

For configuration details and prerequisites, see Spread Zone Configuration.

Erasure parity and storage efficiency

Setting the parity for a deployment is a balance between availability and total usable storage. Higher parity values increase resiliency to drive or node failure at the cost of usable storage, while lower parity provides maximum storage with reduced tolerance for drive/node failures. Use the HyperVault Erasure Code Calculator to explore the effect of parity on your planned cluster deployment.

The following table lists the outcome of varying erasure code parity levels on a HyperVault deployment consisting of 1 node and 16 1TB drives:

Parity Total Storage Storage Ratio Minimum Drives for Read Operations Minimum Drives for Write Operations
EC: 4 (Default) 12 Tebibytes 0.750 12 12
EC: 6 10 Tebibytes 0.625 10 10
EC: 8 8 Tebibytes 0.500 8 9

Summarizing the erasure storage of an object

The HyperVault Client can summarize the current status of an object and all of its shards (or “parts”) across its erasure set. Use mc admin object info to output a summary of the object and the status of each of its shards, including:

  • Part number
  • Pool number
  • Node
  • Erasure set
  • Drive
  • Filename
  • Size

The erasure set must therefore have at least K healthy drives to support read operations. Read quorum Two nodes are offline, leaving twelve readable shards. Read quorum for EC:4 is twelve, so reads still succeed. ERASURE SET N = 16 drives · EC:4 · 2 nodes offline · read quorum K = 12 Parity shard P Data shard D NODE 1 D D NODE 2 D D NODE 3 D D NODE 4 D D NODE 5 D D NODE 6 D D NODE 7 P P NODE 8 P P SHARD AVAILABILITY 12 of 16 shards readable READ QUORUM K=12 · MET Any twelve shards, data or parity, are enough to reconstruct the object. This deployment has two offline nodes, resulting in only 12 remaining healthy drives. The object was written with EC:4 with a read quorum of K=12. This object therefore maintains read quorum and MinIO AIStor can reconstruct it for read operations. MinIO AIStor cannot reconstruct an object that has lost read quorum. You may be able to recover such objects through other means, such as replication resynchronization. MinIO AIStor requires a minimum of K erasure set drives to write an object. The value K here is the write quorum for the deployment. The erasure set must therefore have at least K drives online to support write operations. When parity EC:M is exactly 1/2 the erasure set size, the write quorum is K+1 instead, as described below. Write quorum Two nodes are offline, leaving twelve drives online. Write quorum for EC:4 is twelve, so writes still succeed. ERASURE SET N = 16 drives · EC:4 · 2 nodes offline · write quorum K = 12 Parity shard P Data shard D NODE 1 D D NODE 2 D D NODE 3 D D NODE 4 D D NODE 5 D D NODE 6 D D NODE 7 P P NODE 8 P P SHARD AVAILABILITY 12 of 16 shards readable WRITE QUORUM K=12 · MET AIStor writes all 16 shards and needs K of them acknowledged. This deployment has two offline nodes, resulting in only 12 remaining healthy drives. A client writes an object with EC:4 parity settings where the erasure set has a write quorum of K=12. This erasure set maintains write quorum and MinIO AIStor can use it for write operations. MinIO AIStor always attempts to write all N shards across every drive in the erasure set, not just K. K is a success threshold, not the number of drives MinIO AIStor writes to. For each PUT, MinIO AIStor: Generates all N shards for the object — K data shards plus M parity shards. Dispatches every shard in parallel to its corresponding drive in the erasure set. Waits for a response from every drive, including any drives that fail or time out. Returns success to the client only after at least K drives (or K+1 when M is exactly half the erasure set, see below) acknowledge a successful write. Otherwise, returns failure. For example, a 16-drive erasure set with EC:4 parity always attempts 16 individual drive writes per PUT and tolerates up to 4 unsuccessful writes per object before MinIO AIStor returns an error to the client. A 12-drive erasure set with EC:3 parity attempts 12 drive writes and requires at least 9 to succeed. If parity EC:M is exactly 1/2 the erasure set size, write quorum is K+1. This prevents a split-brain type scenario, such as one where a network issue isolates exactly half the erasure set drives from the other. Losing write quorum but keeping read quorum Four of eight nodes are offline under EC:8, isolating exactly half the drives. Eight shards remain, which meets the read quorum of eight but not the write quorum of nine, so the set serves reads and refuses writes. ERASURE SET N = 16 drives · EC:8 · 4 of 8 nodes offline · half the set isolated Parity shard P Data shard D NODE 1 D D NODE 2 D D NODE 3 D D NODE 4 D D NODE 5 P P NODE 6 P P NODE 7 P P NODE 8 P P SHARD AVAILABILITY 8 of 16 shards readable READ QUORUM K=8 · MET WRITE QUORUM K+1=9 · LOST When parity is exactly half the set, write quorum is K+1 — this is what stops a split brain writing the same object to both halves. This deployment has four of its eight nodes offline due to a transient network failure, isolating exactly half the drives in the erasure set. A client writes an object with EC:8 parity settings where the erasure set has a write quorum of K=9. This erasure set has lost write quorum and MinIO AIStor cannot use it for write operations. However, the erasure set maintains read quorum (K=8) and continues to serve read requests. The K+1 logic ensures that a client cannot write the same object twice, once to each half of the erasure set. When an erasure set loses write quorum but maintains read quorum, MinIO AIStor continues to serve read operations while rejecting write operations until sufficient drives come back online to restore write quorum. When drives are offline at the time of a PUT, MinIO AIStor automatically upgrades parity by default. For each drive that is offline at the time of write, MinIO AIStor increases the object’s parity by one and records the upgraded parity in the object’s metadata. For example, on a 16-drive erasure set with EC:4 parity where 2 drives are offline, MinIO AIStor writes the object as EC:6. This ensures that objects written during a partial outage retain the same level of protection as objects written to a fully healthy erasure set. MinIO AIStor bounds what these upgrades can permanently cost with the MINIO_ERASURE_PARITY_UPGRADE_BUDGET setting, which defaults to 1% of an erasure set’s capacity per outage. You can change this behavior with the MINIO_ERASURE_PARITY_FAILURE setting. See Parity retention optimization for capacity planning considerations and the trade-off against the ignore mode. For an object maintaining read quorum, MinIO AIStor can use any data or parity shard to heal damaged shards. Healing rebuilds the shards that were lost Nodes 5 and 6 are offline, so four data shards are unreadable. Healing rebuilds them from the four parity shards on nodes 7 and 8. ERASURE SET N = 16 drives · EC:4 · 2 nodes offline · 4 data shards lost Parity shard P Data shard D NODE 1 D D NODE 2 D D NODE 3 D D NODE 4 D D NODE 5 D D NODE 6 D D NODE 7 P P NODE 8 P P REBUILD FROM PARITY An object with EC:4 lost four data shards out of 12 due to drive failures. Since the object has maintained read quorum, MinIO AIStor can heal those lost data shards using the available parity shards. Use the MinIO AIStor Erasure Coding Calculator to explore the possible erasure set size and distributions for your planned topology. Where possible, use an even number of nodes and an even number of drives per node. This makes topology planning and drive distribution across erasure sets easier to reason about. Distributing erasure sets across failure domains For Kubernetes deployments, you can configure spread zones so that object data and parity shards spread across separate physical or logical failure domains, such as racks or availability zones. This strategy lowers the risk of one failure affecting multiple shards of the same erasure set. When you configure spread zones, the Operator distributes pods across labeled nodes in a round-robin fashion. For example, with a 16-drive erasure set configured with EC:4 parity and 4 availability zones, the Operator ensures that each zone contains drives from the erasure set, providing protection against zone-level failures. For configuration details and prerequisites, see Spread Zone Configuration. Erasure parity and storage efficiency Setting the parity for a deployment is a balance between availability and total usable storage. Higher parity values increase resiliency to drive or node failure at the cost of usable storage, while lower parity provides maximum storage with reduced tolerance for drive/node failures. Use the MinIO AIStor Erasure Code Calculator to explore the effect of parity on your planned cluster deployment. The following table lists the outcome of varying erasure code parity levels on a MinIO AIStor deployment consisting of 1 node and 16 1TB drives: Parity Total Storage Storage Ratio Minimum Drives for Read Operations Minimum Drives for Write Operations EC: 4 (Default) 12 Tebibytes 0.750 12 12 EC: 6 10 Tebibytes 0.625 10 10 EC: 8 8 Tebibytes 0.500 8 9 Summarizing the erasure storage of an object The AIStor Client can summarize the current status of an object and all of its shards (or “parts”) across its erasure set. Use mc admin object info to output a summary of the object and the status of each of its shards, including: Part number Pool number Node Erasure set Drive Filename Size

title: Healing | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Healing

Healing is HyperVault’s ability to restore an object that has been damaged, corrupted, or partially lost. Damage or loss can come from several sources, including:

  • drive-level errors or failure
  • OS or filesystem errors or failure
  • bit rot

Healing and erasure coding

Whether HyperVault can restore a damaged object depends on three variables:

  • Total drives in the erasure set the object is part of

  • Available drives that contain intact parts of the object

  • Parity settings for the erasure set

Parity specifies how many recovery shards HyperVault creates when it writes an object. The number of data shards is the erasure set size minus the parity. HyperVault distributes shards randomly across the drives in the erasure set, so that no single drive holds only parity shards or only data shards.

HyperVault can use either data or parity shards to reconstruct an object, as long as the number of intact shards is at least the erasure set’s data shard count. HyperVault can then heal the missing data or parity shards while returning the object to the calling client.

Use mc admin object info to summarize the current state of an object on disk. This command outputs a summary of all of the shards of an object (also called “parts”), including any that are missing or damaged.

When does HyperVault heal an object?

Healing during GET and HEAD requests

HyperVault automatically checks the consistency of an object’s data shards each time you request an object with a GET or HEAD operation. For versioned buckets, HyperVault also checks for consistency during PUT operations.

If all of the data shards are found intact, HyperVault serves the object from the data shards without inspecting the corresponding parity shards.

If the object has missing or damaged data shards, HyperVault uses the available parity shards to heal the object before serving it as part of the operation. HyperVault must have at least as many intact shards, of either type, as the erasure set has data shards. Otherwise, HyperVault cannot recover the object. If a parity shard is lost or damaged, HyperVault restores it, provided enough other parity shards remain to serve the object.

Healing with the object scanner

HyperVault uses an object scanner to perform several object-related tasks. One of these tasks checks object integrity and heals any object it finds damaged or corrupted.

On each scanning pass, HyperVault uses a hash of the object name to select one out of every 1,024 objects to check.

If any object is found to have lost shards, HyperVault heals the object from available shards. By default, HyperVault does not check for bit rot corruption using the scanner. This check is expensive to perform, and the risk of bit rot across multiple drives is low.

Consult with HyperVault Engineers before manually starting a healing process on a deployment.

Offline drives

Version added
This behavior was added in HyperVault RELEASE.2025-08-05T18-07-08Z.

When a drive goes offline, HyperVault tracks the duration the drive is offline. If a drive is offline for more than 48 hours, HyperVault also determines whether the erasure set was also offline for the same period.

If both the erasure set and drive were offline for the same period, HyperVault performs no healing. This is because no PUT or DELETE requests would have been possible during the offline time.

If the erasure set remained available for write operations and only the drive was offline, HyperVault heals the objects on the drive. If the drive was offline for more than 48 hours, HyperVault treats the drive as if it were a fresh drive and heals all objects.

Tracking healing status

HyperVault publishes healing metrics under the /cluster/erasure-set endpoint. Use them to monitor the status of healing processes on a deployment.

Bit rot protection

Bit rot is silent data corruption from random changes at the storage media level. For data drives, it is typically the result of decay of the electrical charge or magnetic orientation that represents the data. These sources can range from the small current spike during a power outage to a random cosmic ray resulting in flipped bits. The resulting “bit rot” can cause subtle errors or corruption on the data medium without triggering monitoring tools or hardware.

HyperVault’s optimized implementation of the HighwayHash algorithm captures and heals corrupted objects on the fly. Integrity is ensured from end to end by computing a hash on READ and verifying it on WRITE from the application, across the network, and to the memory or drive. The implementation is designed for speed, so verification adds little to the cost of a read.

You can complete a bit rot scan on a specific object by running mc admin object info with the --bitrot flag.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Debugging and Troubleshooting

Use these tools and techniques to debug HyperVault deployments.

HTTP tracing

Use mc admin trace to capture real-time HTTP API calls to and from the HyperVault server.

Default trace shows only API operation names and HTTP response status:

mc admin trace ALIAS

Trace entire HTTP requests including headers and body:

mc admin trace --verbose ALIAS

Trace all HTTP requests including internode communication:

mc admin trace --all --verbose ALIAS

Trace call types

The --call flag selects which category of operations to trace:

Call type Alias Description
s3 S3 API calls (default)
internal Internal RPC and internode calls
storage Storage I/O calls
os Operating system calls
scanner Background scanner operations
healing heal Healing and recovery operations
ilm Lifecycle management operations
bootstrap Server startup operations
formatting fmt Drive formatting operations
ftp FTP protocol operations
tables HyperVault Tables (Iceberg) API calls
decommission decom Pool decommissioning
rebalance Server pool rebalancing
replication-resync resync Replication resynchronization
batch-replication brep Batch replication operations
batch-keyrotation brot Batch key rotation operations
batch-expiration bexp Batch object expiration

Combine multiple call types with a comma:

mc admin trace --call s3,internal,storage ALIAS

Filter by API operation

Use --funcname to trace specific S3 API operations:

mc admin trace --call s3 --funcname s3.PutObject ALIAS

Combine multiple operations with a comma-separated list:

mc admin trace --call s3 --funcname s3.GetObject,s3.HeadObject ALIAS

Filter by path

Use --path to trace operations on a specific bucket or object:

mc admin trace --call s3 --path "mybucket/path/to/object" ALIAS

Filter by request or response size

Use --filter-request or --filter-response with --filter-size to trace only large operations:

mc admin trace --call s3 --filter-request --filter-size 100MB ALIAS

Filter by HTTP status code

Use --status-code to trace only errors:

mc admin trace --call s3 --status-code 403,500,503 ALIAS

Performance profiling

Use mc support profile to capture CPU, memory, and blocking profiles during a performance issue. Run the profile during the slow period for the most useful data.

mc support profile ALIAS --type cpu,mem,block

Additional profile types: mutex, trace, threads, goroutines, cpuio, runtime, metrics.

Reading profile output

Analyze the downloaded profile files with go tool pprof:

go tool pprof -top profile-NODE-cpu.pprof

Common bottleneck patterns:

Profile pattern Cause Action
High time in syscall.openat / xlStorage.readMetadata Metadata I/O saturation from many objects Enable drive cache (HYPERVAULT_CACHE_ENABLE=on), upgrade for metadata path optimizations
High time in runtime.selectgo / sync.Mutex.Lock Lock contention under high concurrency Upgrade for lock contention fixes, check internode latency
High xlStorage.WalkDir Listing operations scanning large prefixes Reduce prefix depth, check scanner delay setting
runtime.newosproc in crash dump OS thread exhaustion Increase ulimit -u or container pids limit

Drive cache metrics

When drive caching is enabled (HYPERVAULT_CACHE_ENABLE=on), monitor cache effectiveness with Prometheus:

Cache utilization:

sum(hypervault_system_drive_cache_used) / sum(hypervault_system_drive_cache_capacity)

Cache hit ratio:

sum(hypervault_system_drive_cache_hits) / (sum(hypervault_system_drive_cache_hits) + sum(hypervault_system_drive_cache_misses))

Multipart upload troubleshooting

Multipart uploads can stall or accumulate if clients disconnect before completing the upload.

Trace multipart operations

Trace the full lifecycle of multipart uploads in real time:

mc admin trace --call s3 --funcname s3.NewMultipartUpload,s3.PutObjectPart,s3.CompleteMultipartUpload ALIAS

Find large parts being uploaded:

mc admin trace --call s3 --funcname s3.PutObjectPart --filter-request --filter-size 100MB ALIAS

List incomplete multipart uploads 

mc ls ALIAS/BUCKET --incomplete --recursive

Clean up stale multipart uploads

Remove all incomplete multipart uploads older than a specified duration:

mc rm ALIAS/BUCKET --incomplete --recursive --older-than 7d --force

Automate multipart cleanup with lifecycle rules

Set a lifecycle rule to automatically abort incomplete multipart uploads after a number of days:

mc ilm rule add ALIAS/BUCKET --expire-days 7

This prevents stale multipart uploads from accumulating and consuming disk space.

SUBNET health diagnostics

SUBNET health diagnostics collect system information to help ensure the underlying infrastructure is configured correctly. This test is resource-intensive and is recommended at initial deployment and when investigating failure scenarios.

mc support diagnostics ALIAS

The command collects:

  • Admin info
  • CPU information
  • Disk hardware details
  • OS information
  • Memory information
  • Process information
  • Configuration
  • Drive performance
  • Network performance

The output is saved as a compressed JSON file.

The diagnostics output file may contain sensitive information about your environment. Inspect the contents before sharing on any public forum.

Metadata inspection

HyperVault stores object metadata in xl.meta files using a binary format. Use the xl-meta tool to decode these files.

Install xl-meta

Install the xl-meta tool using Go:

go install github.com/hypervault/hypervault/docs/debugging/xl-meta@latest

Use xl-meta

Run xl-meta in a directory containing xl.meta files:

xl-meta ./xl.meta

Decode multiple files recursively:

xl-meta ./**/xl.meta

View inline data stored in metadata:

xl-meta -data xl.meta

Export inline data to a file:

xl-meta --export xl.meta

Remote backend inspection

mc support inspect collects files from all backend drives based on a path pattern. Matching files are collected in a zip file with their respective host, drive, and path information.

Collect xl.meta from a specific object:

mc support inspect ALIAS/bucket/path/to/file.txt/xl.meta

Collect all xl.meta files recursively:

mc support inspect ALIAS/bucket/path/**/xl.meta

Collect part files for all versions of an object:

mc support inspect ALIAS/bucket/path/to/file.txt/*/part.*

The xl-meta tool accepts zip files as input and outputs all xl.meta files found within the archive:

xl-meta inspect.6f96b336.zip

Encrypted inspection

mc support inspect encrypts its output by default, producing an encrypted zip file and a one-time decryption key. No flag is required:

mc support inspect ALIAS/bucket/path/to/file.txt/xl.meta
The decryption key is only shown once and cannot be recovered. The encrypted file can be safely shared without the decryption key.

To produce unencrypted output using the older export method, pass --legacy, which does not encrypt data.

Decryption tool

Install the decryption tool:

go install github.com/hypervault/hypervault/docs/debugging/inspect@latest

Decrypt an inspection file:

inspect -key=<decryption-key> inspect.ad2b43d8.enc

If --key is not specified, an interactive prompt asks for it. The file name contains the beginning of the key to verify the correct key is used.

API version startup errors

A node can fail to start with a fatal API version error after an upgrade or downgrade. These failures are triggered by the API version the cluster runs.

cluster API version could not be determined 

cluster API version could not be determined: .hypervault.sys/api-version is missing or unreadable on all local drives and no node quorum could supply a valid version

The node cannot read a valid API version from its drives and cannot obtain one from a quorum of peers.

To recover:

  1. Confirm that all nodes run the upgraded binary.
  2. Remove the .hypervault.sys/api-version file on all drives.
  3. Restart the cluster simultaneously.

server is older than the data on its drives 

this HyperVault server is older than the data on its drives. The cluster was upgraded to a newer HyperVault release and downgrading to an older release is not supported. Restart the server using the newer HyperVault release that last ran this cluster (on-disk cluster API version <N>, this binary supports up to <M>)

The drives hold a cluster API version newer than this binary can serve, which happens when you attempt to downgrade to an older release after the cluster API version has already bumped.

To recover, restart the server using the newer HyperVault release that last ran the cluster. Downgrade is no longer supported once the API version has been bumped. To retain a rollback window on future upgrades, see Retain a rollback window with a bake time and Downgrading HyperVault versions.

Collect xl.meta from a specific object: mc support inspect ALIAS/bucket/path/to/file.txt/xl.meta Collect all xl.meta files recursively: mc support inspect ALIAS/bucket/path/**/xl.meta Collect part files for all versions of an object: mc support inspect ALIAS/bucket/path/to/file.txt/*/part.* The xl-meta tool accepts zip files as input and outputs all xl.meta files found within the archive: xl-meta inspect.6f96b336.zip Encrypted inspection mc support inspect encrypts its output by default, producing an encrypted zip file and a one-time decryption key. No flag is required: mc support inspect ALIAS/bucket/path/to/file.txt/xl.meta The decryption key is only shown once and cannot be recovered. The file name contains the beginning of the key to verify the correct key is used. API version startup errors A node can fail to start with a fatal API version error after an upgrade or downgrade. These failures are triggered by the API version the cluster runs. cluster API version could not be determined cluster API version could not be determined: .minio.sys/api-version is missing or unreadable on all local drives and no node quorum could supply a valid version The node cannot read a valid API version from its drives and cannot obtain one from a quorum of peers. To recover: Confirm that all nodes run the upgraded binary. Remove the .minio.sys/api-version file on all drives. Restart the cluster simultaneously. server is older than the data on its drives this AIStor server is older than the data on its drives. The cluster was upgraded to a newer AIStor release and downgrading to an older release is not supported. Restart the server using the newer AIStor release that last ran this cluster (on-disk cluster API version <N>, this binary supports up to <M>) The drives hold a cluster API version newer than this binary can serve, which happens when you attempt to downgrade to an older release after the cluster API version has already bumped. To recover, restart the server using the newer AIStor release that last ran the cluster. Downgrade is no longer supported once the API version has been bumped. To retain a rollback window on future upgrades, see Retain a rollback window with a bake time and Downgrading MinIO AIStor versions.

title: Data Recovery | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Data Recovery

Distributed HyperVault deployments rely on Erasure Coding to provide built-in tolerance for multiple drive or node failures. Depending on the deployment topology and the selected erasure code parity, HyperVault can tolerate the loss of up to half the drives or nodes in the deployment while maintaining read access (“read quorum”) to objects.

For Kubernetes deployments, you can further enhance fault tolerance by configuring spread zones to distribute pods across different failure domains, such as racks or availability zones.

The following table lists the typical types of failure in a HyperVault deployment and links to procedures for recovering from each:

Failure Type Description
Drive Failure HyperVault supports hot-swapping failed drives with new healthy drives.
Node Failure HyperVault detects when a node rejoins the deployment and begins proactively healing the data previously stored on that node.
Site Failure HyperVault Site Replication supports complete resynchronization of buckets, objects, and replication-eligible configuration settings after total site loss.

Since HyperVault can operate in a degraded state without significant performance loss, administrators can schedule hardware replacement in proportion to the rate of hardware failure. “Normal” failure rates (single drive or node failure) may allow for a more reasonable replacement timeframe, while “critical” failure rates (multiple drives or nodes) may require a faster response.

Sometimes nodes contain one or more drives that are either partially failed or operating in a degraded state. Symptoms of such drives may include increasing drive errors, SMART warnings, timeouts in HyperVault logs, and so on. You can safely unmount an unhealthy drive if the cluster has sufficient remaining healthy drives to maintain read and write quorum. Missing drives are less disruptive to the deployment than drives that are consistently producing read and write errors.

Changed in RELEASE.2025-02-04T00-52-01Z

If multiple drives within the same erasure set require healing, HyperVault prioritizes the first drive to begin healing within the erasure set. Other drives in the erasure set wait until healing finishes on the first drive before the next drive starts healing.

This allows drives that begin healing to complete the process as quickly as possible.

title: Recover after drive failure | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Recover after drive failure

HyperVault supports hot-swapping failed drives with new healthy drives.

Healing

HyperVault detects and heals those drives without requiring any node or deployment-level restart. HyperVault healing occurs only on the replaced drive(s) and in most cases has minimal or negligible impact on deployment performance.

HyperVault healing ensures consistency and correctness of all data restored onto the drive.

Changed in RELEASE.2025-02-04T00-52-01Z

If multiple drives within the same erasure set require healing, HyperVault prioritizes the first drive that begins healing within the erasure set. Other drives in the erasure set wait until healing finishes on the first drive before the next drive starts healing.

This allows drives that begin healing to complete the process as quickly as possible.

Erasure set healing

Version added
This behavior was added in HyperVault RELEASE.2025-08-05T18-07-08Z.

When a drive goes offline, HyperVault tracks the duration the drive is offline. When a drive is offline for 48 hours or more, HyperVault determines whether the erasure set was also offline.

When an erasure set has remained available, HyperVault may have processed write requests, including both PUT and DELETE requests. As a result, HyperVault heals the disk that has been offline for more than 48 hours as if it were a fresh drive. This allows for the correct writing of all shards that should be on the restored drive.

If the erasure set also went offline during the drive loss, no writes would have been possible. Therefore, no healing is required on the restored drives.

Procedure

The following steps provide a more detailed walkthrough of drive replacement. These steps assume a HyperVault deployment where each node manages drives using /etc/fstab with per-drive labels. On Kubernetes, see Drive replacement on Kubernetes instead.

1) Comment out the failed drive(s)

Open /etc/fstab in your preferred text editor and comment out the drives identified as failed or failing by placing a # at the beginning of the line. For example, the following configuration comments out two failed drives

#/etc/fstab
# <file system>  <mount point>  <type>  <options>         <dump>  <pass>

#LABEL=DRIVE1     /mnt/drive1    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE2     /mnt/drive2    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE3     /mnt/drive3    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE4     /mnt/drive4    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE5     /mnt/drive5    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE6     /mnt/drive6    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE7     /mnt/drive7    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
#LABEL=DRIVE8     /mnt/drive8    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2

Follow your operating system guidance for any additional commands required after updating /etc/fstab.

Commenting the drive ensures that the node can start correctly in the event of a system restart. Do not use nofail or similar methods to force the OS to start with failing drives.

2) Unmount the failed drive(s)

Unmount each failed drive using umount. The following commands assume the device paths /dev/nvme1 and /dev/nvme8 for the two failed drives in the previous example, which are labeled DRIVE1 and DRIVE8:

umount /dev/nvme1
umount /dev/nvme8

3) Replace the failed drive(s)

Remove the failed drive(s) from the node hardware and replace it with known healthy drive(s). Replacement drives must meet the following requirements:

  • Empty, with no data to preserve.
  • Same drive type (for example, HDD, SSD, NVMe).
  • Equal or greater performance.
  • Equal or greater capacity.

Using a replacement drive with greater capacity does not increase the total cluster storage. HyperVault uses the smallest drive’s capacity as the ceiling for all drives in the server pool.

Format each replacement drive as XFS and give it the label of the drive it replaces. Formatting is part of this procedure, so the drive does not need to arrive formatted.

mkfs.xfs /dev/nvme1 -L DRIVE1
mkfs.xfs /dev/nvme8 -L DRIVE8

Use label-based mounting to ensure consistent drive order that persists through system restarts.

4) Update fstab

Open /etc/fstab in your preferred text editor and uncomment the lines associated to the replaced drives:

$ cat /etc/fstab

LABEL=DRIVE1     /mnt/drive1    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE2     /mnt/drive2    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE3     /mnt/drive3    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE4     /mnt/drive4    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE5     /mnt/drive5    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE6     /mnt/drive6    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE7     /mnt/drive7    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2
LABEL=DRIVE8     /mnt/drive8    xfs     defaults,noatime  0       2

If you changed the label used or are using UUID-based mounting, update the label or UUID reference to correspond with the new mount configuration.

Follow your operating system guidance for any additional commands required after updating /etc/fstab.

Cloud environment instances which depend on mounted external storage may encounter boot failure if one or more of the remote file mounts return errors or failure. For example, an AWS ECS instances with mounted persistent EBS volumes may fail to boot with the standard /etc/fstab configuration if one or more EBS volumes fail to mount. You can set the nofail option to silence error reporting at boot and allow the instance to boot with one or more mount issues.

Do not use nofail outside of cloud environments which showcase the aforementioned behavior. Silencing drive errors prevents both HyperVault and the OS from responding to those errors in a normal fashion.

5) Remount the replaced drive(s)

Use mount -a to remount the drives unmounted at the beginning of this procedure:

mount -a

The command should result in remounting of all of the replaced drives. Use df -h or lsblk to verify the result of the mounting operation.

6) Monitor HyperVault for drive detection and healing status

Use mc admin logs command or journalctl -u hypervault for systemd-managed installations to monitor the server log output after remounting drives. The output should include messages identifying each formatted and empty drive.

HyperVault aggressively heals replaced drive(s) to ensure rapid recovery from the degraded state. You do not need to start healing yourself.

To follow its progress, use the healing metrics published under the /cluster/erasure-set endpoint.

Reach for mc admin heal only when you need to inspect a specific bucket or prefix. The command takes a bucket or prefix as a required target, and it returns status only when that target already has a scan running. Otherwise it starts a heal, which is resource intensive and is not normally needed after a drive replacement.

Drive replacement on Kubernetes

The procedure above applies to Linux hosts that mount drives through /etc/fstab. On Kubernetes, where HyperVault DirectPV provisions the storage, the drive-side work uses DirectPV commands and scripts rather than file system edits.

Healing works the same way on Kubernetes. HyperVault detects the replaced drive and heals it, as described under Healing. You do not start healing yourself.

To swap a faulty drive for a new drive on the same node, use the replace.sh script that DirectPV documents under Replace drive. The script first cordons both drives, then the node. Cordoning marks a drive or a node so that it takes no new work. The script then deletes the Pods that use volumes on the faulty drive and moves those volumes to the new drive. It does not move the data on those volumes.

When the move finishes, the script uncordons the new drive and the node. It leaves the faulty drive cordoned and still listed in DirectPV, with no volumes on it. Take that drive out of DirectPV yourself by running kubectl directpv remove with the drive ID. The command accepts any drive that holds no volumes.

Replacing a drive is not the same operation as suspending one. DirectPV suspends a drive so that a StatefulSet can run while the drive is still faulty, and it does not move any volumes. A StatefulSet is active only when all of its Pods run, so a faulty drive prevents the StatefulSet from starting. Running kubectl directpv suspend drives with the drive ID and the required --dangerous flag mounts the volumes on that drive read-only on an empty /var/lib/directpv/tmp directory, which lets the StatefulSet start. DirectPV marks this operation as one that risks data loss. Once you fix the drive, kubectl directpv resume drives with the drive ID returns it to service, and its volumes go back to using it.

Next steps

  • Monitor the cluster for any further drive failures.
  • Some drive batches may fail in close proximity to each other.
  • Deployments seeing higher than expected drive failure rates should schedule dedicated maintenance around replacing the known bad batch.
  • Consider using SUBNET to coordinate with HyperVault engineering around guidance for any such operations.

title: Recover after node failure | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Recover after node failure

If a HyperVault node suffers complete hardware failure (for example, the loss of all drives and data), the node begins healing operations once it rejoins the deployment. HyperVault healing occurs only on the replaced hardware and does not typically impact deployment performance.

HyperVault healing ensures consistency and correctness of all data restored onto the drive.

Changed in RELEASE.2025-02-04T00-52-01Z

If multiple drives within the same erasure set require healing, HyperVault prioritizes the first drive that begins healing within the erasure set. Other drives in the erasure set wait until healing finishes on the first drive before the next drive starts healing.

This allows drives that begin healing to complete the process as quickly as possible.

The replacement node hardware should be substantially similar to the failed node. There are no negative performance implications to using improved hardware.

The replacement drive hardware should be substantially similar to the failed drive. For example, replace a failed SSD with another SSD drive of the same capacity. While you can use drives with larger capacity, HyperVault uses the smallest drive’s capacity as the ceiling for all drives in the server pool.

The following steps provide a more detailed walkthrough of node replacement. These steps assume a HyperVault deployment where each node has a DNS hostname.

1) Start the replacement node

Ensure the new node has received all necessary security, firmware, and OS updates as per industry, regulatory, or organizational standards and requirements.

The new node software configuration must match that of the other nodes in the deployment, including but not limited to the OS and Kernel versions and configurations. Heterogeneous software configurations may result in unexpected or undesired behavior in the deployment.

2) Update hostname for the new node

Optional

This step is only required if the replacement node has a different IP address from the failed host.

Ensure the hostname associated to the failed node now resolves to the new node.

For example, if https://hypervault-1.example.net previously resolved to the failed host, it should now resolve to the new host.

3) Download and prepare the HyperVault server

Follow the deployment procedure to download and run the Object Store using a matching configuration as all other nodes in the deployment.

  • The Object Store version must match across all nodes
  • The HyperVault service and environment file configurations must match across all nodes.

4) Rejoin the node to the deployment

Start the Object Store process on the node and monitor the process output. You can use mc admin logs or the HyperVault service logs using journalctl -u hypervault for systemd managed installations.

The server output should indicate that it has detected the other nodes in the deployment and begun healing operations.

HyperVault aggressively heals the node to ensure rapid recovery from the degraded state. You do not need to start healing yourself.

To follow its progress, use the healing metrics published under the /cluster/erasure-set endpoint.

Reach for mc admin heal only when you need to inspect a specific bucket or prefix. The command takes a bucket or prefix as a required target, and it returns status only when that target already has a scan running. Otherwise it starts a heal, which is resource intensive and is not normally needed after a node replacement.

Next steps

Continue monitoring the deployment until healing completes. Deployments with persistent and repeated node failures should schedule dedicated maintenance to identify the root cause. Consider using SUBNET to coordinate with HyperVault engineering around guidance for any such operations.

title: Recover after site failure | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Recover after site failure

HyperVault can make the loss of an entire site, while significant, a relatively minor incident. Site recovery depends on the replication option you use for the site.

Replication type Restoration method
Site Replication Total restoration of IAM configurations, bucket configurations, and data from the healthy peer site(s)
Bucket Replication Data restoration of objects and metadata from a healthy remote location for each bucket configured for replication
mc mirror Data restoration of objects only from a healthy remote location with no versioning

Site replication healing automatically adds IAM settings, buckets, bucket configurations, and objects from the existing site(s) to the new site with no further action required.

You cannot configure site replication if any bucket replication rules remain in place on other healthy sites. Bucket replication is mutually exclusive with site replication.

If you are switching from using bucket replication to using site replication, you must first remove all bucket replication rules from the healthy site prior to setting up site replication.

Restore an unhealthy peer to site replication

Site replication keeps two or more HyperVault deployments in sync with IAM policies, buckets, bucket configurations, objects, and object metadata. If a peer site fails, such as due to a major disaster or long power outage, you can use the remaining healthy site(s) to restore the replicable data.

The following procedure can restore data in scenarios where site replication was active prior to the site loss. This procedure assumes a total loss of one or more peer sites versus replication lag or delays due to latency or transient deployment downtime.

  1. Remove the failed site from the HyperVault site replication configuration using the mc admin replicate rm command with the --force option.

    The following command force-removes an unhealthy peer site from the replication configuration:

    mc admin replicate rm HEALTHY_PEER UNHEALTHY_PEER --force
    • Replace HEALTHY_PEER with the alias of any healthy peer in the replication configuration
    • Replace UNHEALTHY_PEER with the alias of the unhealthy peer site

    All healthy peers in the site replication configuration update to remove the unhealthy peer automatically. You can use the mc admin replicate info command to verify the new site replication configuration.

  2. Deploy a new HyperVault site following the site replication requirements.

    • Do not upload any data or otherwise configure the deployment beyond the stated requirements.
    • Validate that the new HyperVault deployment functions normally and has bidirectional connectivity to the other peer sites.
    • Ensure the new site matches the server version on the existing peer sites

    The mc admin replicate rm --force command only operates on the online or healthy nodes in the site replication configuration. The removed offline HyperVault deployment retains its original replication configuration, such that if the deployment resumes normal operations it would continue replication operations to its configured peer sites.

    If you plan to re-use the hardware for the site replication configuration, you must completely wipe the drives for the deployment before re-initializing HyperVault and adding the site back to the replication configuration.

  3. Add the replacement peer site to the replication configuration.

    Use the mc admin replicate add command to update the replication configuration with the new site:

    mc admin replicate add HEALTHY_PEER NEW_PEER
    • Replace HEALTHY_PEER with the alias of any healthy peer in the replication configuration
    • Replace NEW_PEER with the alias of the new peer

    All healthy peers in the site replication configuration update for the new peer automatically. You can use the mc admin replicate info command to verify the new site replication configuration.

  4. Resynchronize the new peer with mc admin replicate resync.

    mc admin replicate resync start HEALTHY_PEER NEW_PEER
    • Replace HEALTHY_PEER with the alias of any healthy peer in the replication configuration
    • Replace NEW_PEER with the alias of the new peer

  5. Validate the replication status.

    Use the following commands to track the replication status:

    • mc admin replicate status - provides overall status and progress of replication
    • mc replicate status - provides bucket-level and global replication status

Active bucket replication resynchronization

For scenarios where bucket replication was in place prior to the failure, you can use mc replicate resync to restore data to a new site. Create a new site to replace the failed deployment, then synchronize the data from an existing, healthy, bucket replication-enabled deployment to the new site.

This procedure creates a bucket replication rule, so it carries the same requirements as any other rule. Both deployments must run the same HyperVault version, and versioning must be enabled on the source and destination buckets.

  1. Deploy a new HyperVault site.

  2. Set up IAM and users as needed.

  3. On the new site, create the destination bucket with versioning already enabled.

    mc mb NEWSITE/BUCKET --with-versioning

    Create the bucket this way rather than enabling versioning afterward. Any object written between bucket creation and versioning being enabled receives a null version ID, and replication skips objects with no version ID.

    Confirm that both the source and the destination bucket report versioning as enabled:

    mc version info SOURCE/BUCKET
mc version info NEWSITE/BUCKET

  4. On the site with data, add a replication rule targeting the new site with the mc replicate add command. Pass the remote location to --remote-bucket; HyperVault creates the remote target for you, so you no longer need to determine an ARN first.

    mc replicate add SOURCE/BUCKET                                \
   --remote-bucket 'https://USER:PASSWORD@HOSTNAME:PORT/BUCKET' \
   --replicate "existing-objects,delete,delete-marker"
    Include existing-objects or the resync copies nothing

    mc replicate resync start only processes rules that have existing-object replication enabled. A rule created without existing-objects in --replicate matches no prior objects, so the resync in the next step reports success while copying nothing.

    Every object you are recovering predates the rule, so this flag is what makes the procedure work.

  5. From the site with the data, use the mc replicate resync start command to rebuild the bucket on the new site.

    mc replicate resync start SOURCE/BUCKET \
   --remote-bucket 'NEWSITE/BUCKET'

    Identify the destination with --remote-bucket. HyperVault Client RELEASE.2025-07-28T19-02-30Z and later accepts either ALIAS/BUCKET or the destination ARN. Earlier clients require the ARN.

    Retrieve the ARN with mc replicate ls, which reports it from RELEASE.2025-07-05T15-07-57Z onward. A client older than that can neither pass ALIAS/BUCKET nor look up the ARN, so upgrade it before you start.

  6. Wait for re-synchronization to complete.

    mc replicate resync status SOURCE/BUCKET

    mc replicate resync status reports every remote target for the bucket. Add --remote-bucket to narrow the output to one target.

  7. Set up bucket replication rule(s) from the new HyperVault site to the existing target bucket(s).

  8. (Optional) Delete the bucket replication rules from the target deployment(s) to restore an active-passive replication scenario.

Passive bucket replication resynchronization

Bucket replication can directly restore the site contents by performing a replication from the target bucket(s) to a new HyperVault site.

As a passive process, bucket replication may not perform as quickly as desired for a site recovery scenario.

Bucket replication relies on the standard replication scanner queue, which does not take priority over other processes. For recovery procedures with stricter SLA/SLO, use the active bucket replication process with mc replicate resync command as described above.

Bucket replication rules copy the object, its version ID, versions, and other metadata to the target bucket. HyperVault can restore the object with all of these attributes to a new HyperVault site if bucket replication had already been in use prior to the site loss.

  1. Deploy a new HyperVault site.

  2. Set up IAM and users as needed.

  3. On the remaining target bucket deployment(s), create bucket replication rule(s) for each bucket to the new HyperVault site.

  4. Wait for replication to complete.

  5. Set up bucket replication rule(s) from the new HyperVault site to the existing target bucket(s).

  6. (Optional) Delete the bucket replication rules from the target deployment(s) to restore an active-passive replication scenario.

    Do not delete the bucket replication rules from the deployments used to recover data if you prefer to keep an active-active replication between the buckets. In active-active replication, changes to the objects at either location affect the objects at the other location.

Mirroring

HyperVault’s mirroring copies an object from any S3 compatible storage system.

Mirroring only copies the latest version of each object and does not include versioning metadata, regardless of the source. You cannot restore those attributes with this method.

Use mc mirror in situations where you need to restore only the latest version of an object. Use bucket replication or site replication where those methods were already in use if you are copying from another HyperVault deployment and wish to restore the object’s version history and version metadata.

  1. Deploy a new HyperVault site.
  2. Set up IAM and users as needed.
  3. Create buckets on the new site.
  4. Use the mc cp CLI command to copy the contents from the mirror location to the new HyperVault site.

title: Hotfix Releases | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Hotfix Releases

HyperVault Enterprise-tier subscription customers can receive hotfix releases that backport critical fixes to a specific release version without requiring a full upgrade. Hotfixes allow production environments to remain on a standardized release while receiving targeted patches for bugs, regressions, and security vulnerabilities.

Hotfix backports to a pinned production version are an Enterprise-tier benefit. Enterprise Lite deployments receive fixes by upgrading forward to a current release; see Software Lifecycle and End-of-Life for the support term of each tier.

What is a hotfix

A hotfix is a custom build of HyperVault based on a specific release tag with one or more targeted patches cherry-picked from the upstream codebase. Hotfix releases use the naming convention RELEASE.<date>.hotfix to indicate which base release they are built from.

Hotfixes are delivered as binaries.

What qualifies for a hotfix

HyperVault applies strict criteria for patches eligible for backporting to hotfix branches:

  • Bug fixes that have been reproduced and confirmed in a customer environment.
  • Security fixes that address vulnerabilities affecting the customer’s deployment. HyperVault proactively notifies affected customers through SUBNET when security patches are available.
  • Regression fixes that correct issues introduced in the customer’s current release.

Hotfixes do not include new features, performance enhancements, or changes that alter existing behavior beyond the scope of the fix.

All hotfix patches are first reviewed and merged to the upstream main branch before being backported.

How to request a hotfix

  1. Open a support issue on SUBNET describing the problem, including the release version you are running.
  2. HyperVault Engineering reproduces and validates the issue.
  3. If the fix meets the hotfix criteria, HyperVault creates a hotfix branch from your release tag and backports the patch.
  4. The hotfix binary is built, tested, and delivered to you through the HyperVault download server.

Applying a hotfix

Replace the HyperVault binary with the hotfix version on all nodes and restart:

  1. Download the hotfix binary provided by HyperVault support.

  2. Replace the existing hypervault binary on all nodes in the deployment.

  3. Restart HyperVault on all nodes simultaneously:

    sudo systemctl restart hypervault

HyperVault maintains availability during restarts regardless of the method used. A rolling restart, where nodes are restarted one at a time, offers the added benefit of rollback — if an issue surfaces after the first few nodes, you can revert the remaining nodes to the previous binary before proceeding.

Long-term support

Hotfix branches provide long-term maintenance for production deployments that cannot frequently upgrade. You can continue to receive hotfixes on your standardized release while planning a full upgrade on your own schedule.

When you are ready to upgrade to a newer release, follow the Upgrade procedures. After upgrading, any hotfixes previously applied to the older release are no longer needed, as the newer release includes all upstream fixes.

Subscription requirement

Hotfix releases are available exclusively to HyperVault Enterprise-tier subscription customers. See HyperVault Pricing for subscription details or contact your HyperVault account representative.

Use mc license info to verify your current license and subscription status.
